translations.text: Again, Plerophories, that is, testimonies and revelations that came from God to the saints, concerning the heresy of the two natures and the apostasy that took place at Chalcedon.
Written by one of the disciples of Saint Peter the Iberian, named John, a priest, John Rufus of Antioch, bishop of Maiuma of Gaza.
1. Our blessed father and bishop, Abba Peter the Iberian, used to tell us
that while he was still in Constantinople, before he renounced the world, when Nestorius was still alive and serving as bishop,
during the celebration of the commemoration of the forty holy martyrs in the church called Maria, Nestorius stood up to preach before all the people, near where I was.
He had a womanlike, ringing voice. About halfway through his sermon, he began to blaspheme and say, “Do not boast, Mary,
as though you had given birth to God. For you did not give birth to God, excellent woman, but to a man, an instrument of God.”
As soon as he said this, a demon seized him there on the pulpit, so that his right hand, along with his face, was twisted backward.
As he staggered and was about to fall, the attendants and deacons caught him, carried him away, and brought him into the sacristy.
From that time on, most of the city's people withdrew from communion with him, especially those in the palace. I too did so before all the others, although he loved me very much.
2. The same father also used to tell us about the blessed Pelagius of Edessa, who led a virtuous life.
He was a monk and a prophet. When he heard the blasphemies of Ibas, bishop of Edessa, and openly rebuked him, he suffered greatly at his hands.
When he was persecuted, he came to a place in Palestine and lived in solitude, while Juvenal was still alive, before the council and the apostasy from the faith.
Grace dwelt in him so fully that he was filled with the spirit of prophecy and was considered worthy to see visions frequently.
He used to visit Abba Peter regularly, who was then living in solitude in the monastic settlement of Maiuma of Gaza, because of the great love they had for one another.
One day, while he was walking with the father in the sandy areas of the monastic settlement and discussing thoughts and virtues according to God,
he said that he had fallen into a trance and, seven years before the council, had seen the apostasy that the bishops would commit at Chalcedon.
He also spoke the name of the wicked emperor Marcian, in whose days and through whose actions it would take place, and described the other events one by one.
He said, “That time will overtake both me and you, Abba. We will be persecuted together with all the saints
who refuse to consent to the abandonment of the faith, and we will end our lives in that very persecution.” This was indeed what happened in the end.
3. Our father used to tell us that this same Abba Pelagius the prophet, while our father and other holy men were near the elder,
had another vision before the council and began to say with tears, “Woe, Pulcheria! Woe, Pulcheria! Woe, Pulcheria!”
When we pleaded with him very insistently to explain what he was saying, he said, “Pulcheria, who pledged her virginity to God and deposed Nestorius,
to whom all the saints everywhere used to write as to a holy woman and virgin who stood in defense of orthodoxy,
will betray both the faith and her virginity and crush the saints.” This indeed happened: she broke the vows of chastity that she had made to Christ.
And she married Marcian and became heir to his kingdom, his wickedness, and the torments reserved for him.
4. Again, this same Pelagius the priest, as Pamphilus, a deacon of the church of Jerusalem who was his friend, related,
once went in with him to pray at the holy place of Golgotha while it was still night, for this was his custom. While he stood praying,
he was caught up in a vision. Overcome by grief and tears, he began saying, “Juvenal! Juvenal! Juvenal!” Finally, when he emerged from the vision,
the deacon Pamphilus fell before him in private and asked him what the vision meant and why he had kept crying out, “Juvenal!”
He said, “If you live, you will see Juvenal being escorted in procession by Romans and demons,
just as you now see Juvenal being escorted in procession by monks and clergy.”
5. This same man, seeing in the Spirit what was to come, used to say to the holy Abba and the blessed John the eunuch, “Study the divine Scriptures, my sons,
and when Christ entrusts his churches to you, pray for me.” Thus he foretold their ordination.
The blessed Abba Peter was astonished and took no pleasure in what was being said, since he fled even from the very mention of ordination.
Distressed, he said to the old man, “You do not know what you are saying, old man!” But Pelagius cheerfully replied,
“I know what I am saying. Whoever wishes to be distressed may be distressed!”
6. During the time of apostasy from the faith, he constantly offered this prayer: “Lord my God,
keep me unwavering in the true faith until the end, and keep me from entering into communion with those who betrayed the faith at Chalcedon.
Take my spirit wherever you wish and however you wish, even in a tavern or an inn. Only keep me from falling away.” And this indeed happened.

For in Ascalon there was a certain Cyril, a tavern keeper of the true faith, who had been driven out of Maiuma because of his orthodoxy. He had moved to Ascalon and was working there as a tavern keeper.
While the blessed Pelagius was fleeing and hiding with him, he died there one night, in accordance with his prayer and prophecy.
When some of the zealous brothers of Maiuma learned of this, they came by night, took his body, and buried him in the laura, in the monastery of the Christ-loving Aaron, the wheat merchant.
On that very night when he died, while the bishops of the true faith were being persecuted,
Abba Peter the bishop had moved away and was staying in Oxyrhynchus in the Thebaid. From so great a distance,
he saw the blessed Pelagius in a vision, coming to him joyfully and with a cheerful face. He greeted him and said, “Abba, pray for me and commend me,
for I am departing to the Lord.” Abba Peter recorded the day on which he had seen the vision,
and later discovered that it was the very day on which the great confessor Pelagius had died. His mother, who observed week-long fasts,
conceived, bore, and raised him in holiness. When he had grown into a man and come of age, one of the city's distinguished men died, and he saw him being carried in a funeral procession.
He was deeply stricken in soul and immediately fled from that funeral procession to a monastery, having recognized the folly of this world. Thus he became a chosen vessel.
7. The blessed John, a priest of Alexandria, known as John of the house of Tatiana, a well-known and distinguished man, told us: “When I was young,
I had a desire to renounce the world. Since I was accustomed to visiting Abba Alidius, the prophet of the Cells, I hurried to him to reveal my desire to him
and learn from him whether the Lord would bring my desire and aspiration to fulfillment. I asked him to pray for me. But he said, ‘Wait for now.
For I see no urgency at present. Instead, go and live quietly, taking care to make progress in a virtuous way of life.
For after a certain time, persecution will come upon the church. Then you will flee and come here and become a monk.’
When I said to Abba Alidius, ‘What persecution? Is paganism going to take hold?’ he told me, ‘No. But a wicked emperor named Marcian will arise,
and he will make the bishops declare in writing that the one who was crucified is not God.
When all these obey him and submit, the bishop of Alexandria alone—
I mean Dioscorus—will not obey him. Because of this, he will be persecuted and sent into exile, and there he will die.’
When I said to him, ‘Will the people of Alexandria allow him to go into exile?’ he told me, ‘Yes, for he will be forced out, and another man, a denier of the faith, will take his place.’
When I became distressed at what had been said, he said, ‘But God will raise up for himself in those days
a priest who does his will.’ He was referring to the blessed Timothy. ‘And the man before him, who took power like a tyrant, will be killed,’ he said,
referring to the wicked Proterius. ‘But Timothy himself, after remaining in the episcopate for a few days,
will be cast into exile.’ When the old man had said this and fallen silent, I became deeply distressed and said, ‘My lord abba,
will that orthodox bishop then remain in exile, while the city and all Egypt perish and wickedness takes hold?’
But he remained silent. When I persisted in pleading with him, he told me, ‘If there is time, he will return. After remaining a little while,
he will die in the true faith.’ When he had said this and fallen silent, I fell down before him, wanting to learn from him what would happen afterward.
But he said, ‘What you have heard so far is enough for you. After these things, the time of the Antichrist will arrive.’”
8. The blessed Zeno, the wandering monk and prophet from Kfar Searta—a village in Palestine—also foretold this same thing
to Abba Stephen, a monk who later became a deacon of Jerusalem, before the Council of Chalcedon.
For Stephen wished to go and live in a foreign land for God’s sake and to share in the virtue of living away from his homeland.
For this reason he came to Abba Zeno and asked whether the Lord would bring his aspiration to fulfillment. He heard him say,
“For now, go and live quietly. For persecution and an uprising of heretics are going to come upon the church because of the orthodox faith.
Then you will leave for a foreign land even against your will, if you wish to remain orthodox.”
This indeed happened to him: in the end he moved to a foreign land, and there he died, because of the Council of Chalcedon.
Now the blessed Zeno had the custom of receiving all the monks who came from every place,
listening to the thoughts of each one of them, and telling each one what would lead to salvation.
Finally, foreseeing the evils that would overtake the inhabited world because of the apostasy that was to take place at Chalcedon,
he shut himself away a year before the apostasy and no longer received anyone.
He spent that year before the council of the apostates in mourning and sighing.
400. Abba Innocent of Pamphylia used to tell us this.
He was a chaste man and a leader of the brothers. He said that in Pamphylia there was a large, deep ravine, where one of the holy ascetics
once, before the council, saw the devil come to him and say, “Fall down and worship me.” When the holy man blew at him and rebuked him,
that filthy demon went away, saying to him, “Why have you refused to worship me? Look, I am gathering all the bishops
and holding a council. There all the bishops will worship me.”
10. Perhaps what is about to be told will seem unbelievable and astonishing to some.
But chaste men, elders worthy of trust, and holy monks told it to me and to those who were then staying in Abba Romanus’s monastery,
when they gathered for his commemoration: Abba Atarbius, a man who did not lie; Abba Pergamius;
Abba Thomas Dougius, the foremost disciple of Abba Romanus; and many other elders with good consciences.
They did not conceal the sign that occurred in Palestine, which foretold the bishops’ apostasy.
For when the unlawful council was about to take place, the sky suddenly grew gloomy, with darkness and thick clouds.
Sticks of eye salve rained down in the holy city, in all the villages around it, and in many places in Palestine.
They were alike in shape in every respect and resembled those made by people. They bore various ugly impressions,
so that many people gathered them. Some who used them unknowingly were blinded. People said that Hesychius, the preacher of Jerusalem,
collected many of them, showed them to Empress Eudocia, and sent some to Constantinople as evidence of that sign,
which foretold the blindness that would seize the world because of the bishops’ apostasy, as the prophet Isaiah said: “God’s servants have become blind.”

A great deal of fine dust could be seen beneath the sticks of eye salve, as evidence that they had descended from above. Some people who lived nearby said that even now a basket full of them was still preserved in the village of Gath.
Our blessed father Peter also testified to these things, saying that in those days he had heard a clear account of this sign from those who had seen it,
while he was then living in seclusion in the monastery of Maiuma. His disciple Abba Andrew also affirmed
that he himself had seen these three things with his own eyes: this sign of the sticks of eye salve, and that Samaritan who had previously been blind and regained his sight;
The man who rubbed his eyes with some of the blood of the holy monks who were killed near Neapolis at the time of the apostasy.
And the Eucharistic offering that visibly became blood and flesh in the Church of the Apostles at Caesarea, when the holy orthodox fathers went
to meet Juvenal the apostate as he returned from the council, to rebuke him or persuade him to repent and set himself right.
They were prevented by the governor from entering Caesarea because they were a large crowd. And when a large crowd poured out toward them,
he persuaded them to celebrate the Eucharist in the Church of the Apostles outside the city.
When many believers took some of this offering and kept it with them, they later found it to be real flesh and blood.
Abba Maxus the priest, a trustworthy man, also testified to this miracle, saying that he himself had witnessed such a mystery.
But if anyone does not accept this sign that occurred, which equals the miracle of those who anointed themselves,
let him accept its confirmation when he learns what happened then that resembles it, which is acknowledged by everyone and attested in the public document.
For on the very day when the wicked Marcian was raised to imperial power and put on the crown, suddenly
darkness seized the whole inhabited world, with [?] thick gloom and falling dust. The darkness was like the darkness that seized Egypt.
For it darkened the air so much that all the inhabitants of the imperial city
were filled with great fear and confusion everywhere and mourned. They wailed loudly and lamented, as though the end were swiftly approaching.
This was a prophecy of the darkness that was going to come upon the whole inhabited world through the hands of the tyrant himself,
and of blindness and darkness concerning the fear of God, so that the whole creation, one might say, was mourning beyond words.
It was announcing beforehand the denial of God that would take place, and the oppression of the orthodox faith by the wicked emperor himself
and by so great an assembly of bishops from the inhabited world. This darkness lasted until evening.
The proof, testimony, and unquestionable confirmation of these things do not come from an outside source,
but from the very writings of the tyrant who fights against God, which were publicly posted. For when he saw the confusion and [?] among the soldiers and throughout the city,
and that everyone was taking his reign as an omen, as though it would bring great calamities upon the whole world,
he became afraid and deeply disturbed. He promptly posted public documents, attempting to conceal the wrath that came from God,
and imagining that he could deceive the peoples. For he said the opposite, as the document itself teaches those who read it:
“The whole world should expect an abundance of great blessings from my reign, since the darkness of the emperor who preceded me is being driven away,
as it receives the light of the excellence of my rule.” And this was the beginning and first of his decrees.
This document, when it was posted throughout the whole world, was a rebuke and a sure demonstration to those who had ears to hear, eyes to see, and a heart to understand.

And the written [?] is the one that immediately and without delay, through the zeal of his tyranny, encountered the transgression and estrangement from God that came about through the bishops of Chalcedon.
11. For another such sign also occurred in those days in Jerusalem, foretelling the offense against God.
For the venerable cross, which was large, had shone and gleamed for many years at the holy place of the Ascension.
When it was suddenly scorched by fire and thrown to the ground, it shook the hearts of all who feared God,
so that the God-fearing Empress Eudocia had a bronze one made in its place to comfort and reassure the people.
This is the one that can still be seen shining today; it contains six thousand pounds of bronze.
12. Once Abba Peter the bishop had a conversation with Abba Isaiah, who was living in solitude in the [?] of Dodekata,
in the presence of our brothers Zachariah and Andrew, the cell companions—I mean those of Abba Peter.
They used to tell us what Abba Isaiah himself had said. He said, “I know that once I visited one of those great saints,
who was Abba Paul the Theban. He had already grown old and was about a hundred and twenty years of age.
And I heard this prophecy from him: ‘After twenty years there will be an apostasy on the part of the bishops,
that is, the estrangement from God which the apostle foretold. It will come about through a wicked man who will become emperor, whose name is Marcian.
That emperor will die after six years and a little more. After him a deceitful man will appear for a short time, bring a measure of peace to the churches, and then cease.
And so affairs will drag on until the coming of the Antichrist.’”
13. In agreement and harmony with this prophecy is the one given by Abba Zeno, who was called “Three Cells.”
He lived in solitude at the Enaton of Alexandria, as the distinguished lawyer Epinetetes related. For he said, “When I was in Alexandria,
and was still a young man studying there, it was my practice, out of faith, to visit the elder frequently.
Once, when I went to him as usual and unexpectedly came to his cell, I saw him sitting with a cord in his hands and his eyes fixed upward.
Thinking that he was praying, I waited a little for him to finish his prayer. But when he remained motionless for a long time,
I thought to myself, ‘God has revealed my sins to the elder, and that is why he does not speak with me or welcome me warmly.’
After I had waited a little longer and the elder still remained absorbed in the vision, I turned around as though about to leave.
But he called out loudly to me, ‘Why are you leaving?’ I knelt and bowed before him. Without saying anything else to me, he said, ‘Go and write.’
At that time the blessed orthodox Archbishop Timothy was in exile. The elder said, ‘After a certain number of years,
the blessed Timothy will return from exile and restore orthodoxy. After two years he will die.
After him his archdeacon will become bishop, and in his days there will be a division in the churches that will not be healed until the coming of the Antichrist.’”
14. Abba Paul, who had been a sophist and lived with Abba Andrew, an elder and prophet, also told us this.
He was a hardworking and steadfast man who, before the council, had been one of those great saints of Egypt.
While in a vision, he saw a large gathering of bishops heating a furnace with great ferocity.
They threw a beautiful little child, who resembled light, into it. They plastered the furnace shut on every side, so that not even smoke could be seen coming from it,
nor could any air enter it. After three days he saw the little child come out of the furnace unharmed, and he recognized that it was the Lord.
As someone accustomed to speaking with him, he said to him, “Lord, who are these people who did this to you and threw you into the furnace?”
He answered him, “The bishops have crucified me again, and they have plotted to rob me of my glory.” And he spoke rightly.
For the Nestorians suffer from the disease of the Jews: they say that the one who was crucified was a mere human being, and not God who became flesh.
Then, as the elder looked again, he saw an old man standing at a distance, who neither agreed with those other bishops nor joined them,
either when they heated the furnace or when they threw the child in and sealed it shut. The elder said to the child,
“Who is this old man?” He answered, “He is Dioscorus, archbishop of Alexandria,
who alone did not take part in their schemes.” Then the elder, as though given freedom to speak, took courage and said to the Lord, “My Lord,
how does this come about, that the bishops of Alexandria struggle so fiercely for the truth, even to death?”
He answered, “It dates from when Simon of Cyrene carried my cross. Now Cyrene belongs to the region of Egypt.
From that time it was prophetically known beforehand that Egypt—to which Cyrene, situated in Libya, belongs—was destined
to carry my cross and follow me until the end, and to show zeal for me even to death.”
15. To confirm this and provide full assurance, it is necessary to add to the account what I heard
from the man who went into exile with the blessed Timothy and was near the holy man at his passing.
He heard him recount it in his own voice. For he related that when the blessed Timothy was about to reach the end of his life,
he summoned the leading members of the clergy and said to them, “Even if I am acting foolishly, as the blessed apostle says,
nevertheless, I think it necessary, for your warning and for knowledge and understanding of this time that has arrived, to tell you something that happened to me when I was a little boy
and was going to school in the morning. An old man met me, gentle, chaste, and worthy of God.
He took hold of my head with his hands and kissed me with a cheerful and radiant face, saying to me, ‘Greetings to you, Timothy, bishop of the end.’
After saying this three times, he disappeared, and I never saw him again, right up to the end.”
16. Once, while I was living in Jerusalem, I happened to make a journey along the road leading from Siloam down into the valley, to the places beyond it.
Now a well-known man from among the city's inhabitants, who knew these places, was traveling with me. And when I looked toward the left side of the road,
I saw beneath the hill there a large monastery, dilapidated and falling down, with various trees around it. Some of them were dry,
while others had grown wild and become thorny. The vineyard there had likewise become useless. In amazement, I said to the man traveling with me,
“I am astonished that, although all these visitors come to Jerusalem and eagerly seek out many properties
to buy and build themselves monasteries and places of solitude, this place has remained uninhabited and fallen into ruin. Whose is it, then?”
He brightened up and said about it, “This monastery belonged to Juvenal. While he was living here in solitude, he became bishop.
And after the Council of Chalcedon took place, it unexpectedly fell into such ruin, as though struck by the wrath of God.
Through its collapse, this place became, as you see, uninhabitable and utterly ruined, so that no one can live in it.”
Filled with amazement, I sighed and said, “Truly Juvenal was a companion of Judas, as the blessed Dioscorus said about him.
That is why this place has inherited the curse of Judas. Of him the Spirit-inspired Scripture says, ‘Let his dwelling become desolate, and let no one live in his tents.’”
17. I also remember hearing this, together with many others, from our father Abba Peter.
Juvenal used to make the rounds of the monasteries around the holy city during these forty holy days,
visiting those who practiced asceticism in them, according to the ancient custom. He also came to a certain elder, one of those venerable and great ascetics who were close to God.
When the elder learned that he was approaching, he shut the door of his cell, bolted it, and remained quietly inside.
When Juvenal arrived, accompanied by clergy from the city, they knocked at the door, but he did not open it.
When they persisted and threatened either to climb over the wall or to break down the door, the elder began shouting,
“Antichrist, go away from me! I will not allow the Antichrist to enter my cell! Judas the betrayer shall not enter here!”
He said many other things like these. Those who were with Juvenal grew angry,
but at the same time they were ashamed at what was being said. Juvenal told them, “Leave him alone.
He is out of his mind. Excessive asceticism has dried up his brain, and he does not know what he is saying.” These things were reported throughout the whole city
and its surrounding region. All who heard waited to see what would happen, knowing that this elder
was a holy man and a friend of God, filled with spiritual grace, and that he did not say anything without reason.
18. Another similar event also happened in those days, as our father Peter himself told us. At that time he was still living in Jerusalem,
and he himself witnessed what happened. He said that in the church called the Probatica, at the pool where the Lord healed the paralyzed man,
a certain young reader, one of those assigned to serve there, was carrying out his day's duties and was present early in that holy place.
He clearly saw our Lord and God Jesus entering there in glory, accompanied by a company of saints.
When he saw the lamps of the church, some extinguished and others carelessly tended, he cried out and said:
“What am I to do with these people? I lavish such good things on them—oil and wine and all the other necessities.
They never lack anything that could give them an excuse to be negligent and careless in my service.
Alas for Juvenal! He has made my house a den of robbers and filled it with fornicators, adulterers, and defiled people.”
As he was saying this, he entered the sacristy and ordered the cupboards containing the sacred vessels to be opened.
When he saw that these too were being neglected, along with other similar things, he cried out and said to those who were with him:
“You yourselves take them and wash them thoroughly. Sprinkle [?] over them and put them away properly.”
After this was done, as he was leaving the sacristy, he saw that reader cowering and hiding in fear. He said:
“What is this man doing here? Put him out of here!” But the man fell on his face and said, “Have mercy on me!” The Lord said to him, “Get out of here!
I do not know your deeds.” But when the man persisted in pleading, the Lord said to him, “Will you repent now and stop being negligent?”
He replied, “If your mercy helps me, I will do what I can.” And so, when the Lord departed,
from that day onward he remained in astonishment and immeasurable mourning, gripped by inexpressible groans. When day came,
the ministers of that church and the people of the neighborhood came running. When they saw him mourning and trembling like this, they kept asking him to explain the reason.
He openly told them the whole vision he had seen, offering the sacred vessels themselves as confirmation of what he was saying.
For when they opened the cupboards, they found the vessels shining with divine radiance. Something like dust had been sprinkled over them instead of [?],
which was extraordinary and wonderful, with a splendid and pleasant fragrance as well. Thus, when news of this spread throughout the city,
crowds of people came running there. I too went with my brother John, now at rest, and we witnessed this remarkable wonder.
But when Juvenal heard this, he could not bear the disgrace and reproach of what was being said about him, for none of it had happened in secret.
At night he seized the man who had seen these things and made him disappear. How and where, God knows. The blessed Peter also used to say this:
“I know a man among those blessed people who live in solitude in the holy city.” Whether he was speaking about himself or someone else, he did not make entirely clear.
He said, “I know this man: when he had a vision in the days of Juvenal and saw the abominations taking place inside the sanctuary,
from that day onward he would not enter the church with him or receive Communion from his hand. Instead, he received it privately in the sacristy.
For the transgression at Chalcedon had not yet occurred.” But he did not tell us who the holy man was who had seen this vision.
19. But our blessed father, the truthful man of God, used to add this to the account:
For he could not endure the shameful things being done by Juvenal, his relatives, and his personal attendants, and he saw how many people were being led astray.
And amid the crowds of visitors who came there from everywhere, as though prompted by divine inspiration, he shut himself up alone in his cell from the ninth hour onward.
He threw himself down before God with bitter tears and mourning, repeatedly bending his knees and standing up.
He would speak as though in the person of God, saying, “What should I have done for human beings that I have not done for their salvation?
I established heaven. I laid the foundations of the earth. I planted paradise. I brought forth all creation for their enjoyment. And after Adam’s transgression,
I gave the law. I sent patriarchs and prophets. I performed countless signs and wonders to persuade them.
Finally, I sent my only Son for their sake. When he came to them, he proclaimed the kingdom of heaven and granted forgiveness of sins.
He healed their sick. He made the blind see and the lame walk. He drove out demons. For their sake he was crucified. For their sake he died.
Having abolished death, he rose from the dead and confirmed the hope of resurrection. When he ascended to heaven, he sent the Spirit. He sent out apostles and evangelists.
He overthrew idols. Yet in return for all these things, they reject me and my laws, trample on my commandments, and abandon my faith.
Look, their house is left to them desolate.” After this vision, he never ceased to perform this same service every day.
Alone, he continued offering up this same mourning for a long time, with words like these and with tears, until the time of the transgression that took place at Chalcedon was about to draw near.
20. Ganta is a village situated fifteen miles north of the Holy City. It formerly belonged to Empress Eudocia,
but now, under the terms of her will, it belongs to the church of Jerusalem. In this village there was a priest named Paul, a native of the village,
who had loved the ascetic life from his youth and was adorned with every virtue taught in the gospel: holiness, virginity, chastity, love for the poor,

and hospitality to strangers. He was honored by all the people and by the empress herself, and was chosen in God’s sight. In that village he established a cenobium—that is, a large and conspicuous monastery.
He became the father of a large community of monks. Eventually, however, the inhabitants of the village took him away from them,
and he became the priest of the village church. Concerning him, people who knew the man personally affirm
that throughout all those years when he gathered the village together, men and women alike, he practiced, along with his other virtues, the discipline of never looking at a woman’s face.
When Lady Eudocia learned this and verified it through her own experience, she received communion from him alone until her death,
and from no one else—not from a bishop, nor from a cleric, nor even from someone who was a monk.
Our blessed father Peter also bore witness to this man’s godly virtue, for he loved him very deeply and was closely attached to him.
When the council at Chalcedon, the council of those who rejected us, was assembling, this blessed Paul had a vision at night. He saw a vast plain
that contained, so to speak, all humanity. In the middle of the plain he saw a high hill, and above the hill a canopy
supported by columns of gold and silver. In its center stood an altar fashioned from precious stones and fine pearls.
And it was sending out indescribable rays. Around it was a great gathering of saints, standing and ministering at the altar.
Among them, as he said, he recognized some people who were still alive at that time. And a voice came from heaven, saying:
“Accursed is anyone who speaks of two natures.” And those who were standing around the altar, and they alone, answered in a loud voice:
“Amen.” But the crowds that filled the plain stood silently in fear and trembling, amazed.
And again that divine voice cried out: “Accursed is anyone who divides the one who is indivisible. Accursed are the deniers.”
And they alone answered, “Amen.” When these visions had ceased, the old man came to himself, gripped by great distress and sighing.
He was thinking and pondering whether something that would cause people to stumble had come from the Council of Chalcedon and from Juvenal.
For that unholy man had also stopped at his monastery while going up to the imperial court. Juvenal had shown him honor,
because he saw that Empress Eudocia had great confidence in him. And he had said to the old man:
“I have stopped to see you because I do not expect to see you again. For we are going up to a struggle, and exile awaits us, unless we trample on our conscience before God.
For they demand that we betray and deny the faith of our fathers and adopt the views of Simon the Magician and the Jews,
as though Christ, who suffered for us, were not God. So pray for us, my lord and father, that I may not be put to shame in my old age.”
So, as the old man remembered these things and thought about the vision in amazement, he did not know what to do.
Again, at night, he saw Juvenal standing in a corner, naked and hiding himself in shame.
He was blackened all over like the soot of a furnace, with a filthy loincloth full of patches wrapped around him [?]. The old man cried out to him in a loud voice and said:
“My lord archbishop, what is this that has happened to you? What does this clothing you are wearing signify?” But he said, “What can I do about my sins?
Look, you see my shame. I am gathering a great deal of gold for the Antichrist, because he is going to wage war against the dust.”
When the old man awoke, he marveled at the vision and concluded that nothing good had happened at the council, but rather something that would cause people to stumble.
He awaited the outcome to confirm his certainty. And when the denial of the faith was proclaimed everywhere, the old man marveled at the vision that had come to him.
And as the old man sought to understand what Juvenal had said to him in the vision about the Antichrist, who was going to wage war against the dust,
he understood, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, that “against the dust” clearly meant against humanity, which is of dust and was formed from the earth.
And all those who are earthly and cling to the earth—these are the ones the Antichrist will seize and conquer, and these are the ones he will lead astray.
21. From this point onward, I am compelled to tell a shocking and fearful account to establish the truth, with the true God as my witness,
since I myself came to know it through reliable testimony: I heard the truth from those who had seen it, and I was left in no doubt.
There is a city in Isauria called Titiopolis, because it was rebuilt several times by Emperor Titus.
Its bishop was named Phanoprepius, a chaste man and a cenobiarch, that is, head of the monastery that was in that region.
He was forcibly taken from the monastery and accepted the episcopal ministry of that city. Now, when the council was held at Chalcedon,
Basil, metropolitan of the city of Seleucia in Isauria, took him along with the other bishops when he went to the council.
When he came to the council, he saw the struggle that most of the bishops were waging for the truth at the outset.
Virtually all of them were anathematizing those who spoke of two natures,
and they agreed with the blessed Dioscorus. They would accept neither Leo’s Tome nor those who had been justly deposed: Flavian, Ibas, and Theodoret.
But when he then saw their subsequent downfall and denial of the faith, and Dioscorus, the champion of the truth, deposed by them,
while those previously mentioned heretics and fighters against God were received without a hearing and contrary to the canons, and recovered their sees,
he withdrew to his lodgings. Shutting himself in, he kept vigil with tears and groans. He cried out to our Lord, saying, “God of truth and Savior of the ages,
true light, my hope since my youth, do not let me, your servant, fall away from hope in you and become an outcast and a denier of the faith in my old age.
Instead, make your will known to me. Because I am unlearned, and many are falsifying the truth, reveal to me your unerring judgment
concerning what has happened at this council: whether it has happened according to your will, and which people are acceptable to you—
Dioscorus, archbishop of Alexandria, whom they deposed, or these others,
who received those aforementioned wicked men without a hearing and ratified Leo’s Tome—so that, receiving full assurance through your grace,
I may stand firm in the truth without doubt or fear, even to the shedding of blood, and not betray the faith of my fathers and my hope in you.”
And so, after he had spent three days and nights kneeling before the Lord and pleading, he saw a vision like this: a large scroll of papyrus,
unrolled from heaven and descending all the way to the earth. On both sides, here and there, it was written in large letters:
“This council is accursed. They have denied me! They have denied me! They are accursed, accursed!” When he saw this vision,
he received great assurance, without any doubt. Immediately, during the night, he left everyone behind, departed, and went to his city.
When he arrived there, he gathered all the people of the city and told them everything that had happened at Chalcedon,
how the bishops had renounced orthodoxy, and how he had received assurance about this from heaven. He testified to them, saying,
“For this reason I made every effort to hurry here first and make the truth known to you, so that you would not be subjected to any deception or error.
If you are prepared to stand firm with me, unshaken in the orthodox faith,
and to follow me and flee from these deniers of the faith and their Eucharistic offering, I am ready to remain with you
and fight for your salvation even to the shedding of blood, and, if necessary, lay down my life for you. But if you have it in mind
that you enter into communion with Basil the metropolitan and with those who agree with him in their thinking. I clear myself of responsibility for your blood.
But I am saving and rescuing my own soul. And when he had thus set their hearts ablaze with love for God and zeal for the truth,
he continued afterward for seventeen years as bishop, guarding his flock with blameless integrity
and without departing from the orthodox faith. And this despite being severely tried by dangers and plots,
both by Basil himself, the metropolitan of Isauria, and by the man who was called patriarch of the city of Antioch.
For these men were supporters of the false doctrine of Chalcedon. Yet, through God's protection and grace, he remained unwavering, unshaken, and unchanged,
and guarded his flock. And so he departed gloriously to God, his Savior Christ, crowned with the crown of confession.
It is therefore necessary for me, to strengthen those who hear, to relate how I came to have such assurance.
22. Peter, who became archbishop of Antioch at the time of the Encyclical, and from whom I also received ordination to the priesthood, unworthy though I am,
when he returned from exile to Antioch and assumed the office of chief bishop, sent his synodical letter to the leader of God's holy church in Jerusalem—
this was Martyrius—by the hand of a certain man named Peter, a bishop.
This man was an Isaurian by birth, from the previously mentioned Titiopolis.
He administered the bishopric as a disciple and cell companion, and was the successor of the universally renowned and blessed confessor, Bishop Paneuprepius.
For he was considered worthy to receive that man's episcopal office, and was expected to show zeal equal to his
on behalf of the orthodox faith. He also sent with him a certain priest of the church of Antioch,
whose name was Solomon and who was Armenian by birth. He had once been a cell companion both to him and to my humble self,
and I loved him dearly. He instructed them to use every means to persuade my weak self to return to him.
For after his exile and the takeover by the heretics, I had left the city of Antioch
and had been granted the privilege of associating with the holy fathers in Palestine, especially my father and superior, the hospitable Abba Peter, the Iberian bishop,
and the great ascetic Abba Isaiah. Having found abundant delight in the embrace of the holy man, I sent back word
that from then on I would live in Palestine and would not be separated from their faith, hope, and spiritual benefit.
I was living in seclusion in Jerusalem, where at that time a large community of orthodox fathers
had a dwelling and cells for seclusion. But when those who carried the synodical letters came to the holy city—
I mean Peter, bishop of Titiopolis, and Solomon the priest—and, after searching diligently, found my humble self,
they pressed me urgently and relentlessly, compelling me and insisting that they must take me with them by every means, while also presenting me with many [?].
That is, provisions for the journey and letters from Archbishop Peter, which were full of great joy and appeals.
They also added this to their appeals: “We have instructions from him, for your full assurance, to persuade you by every means to come to him, for he says:
‘Just let him come to me so that we can see one another. Give him your word that no one will compel him to receive communion unless he is persuaded.
Rather, I will send him away in peace.’” I promptly made these things known to my holy father and savior after God, Abba Peter the Iberian,
who was then staying in the region near the city of Ashkelon, imploring and urging him
to send me whatever brief reply he thought appropriate. After a few days I received this answer from him: Letter of Saint Peter the Iberian.
“When we read the letter from Your Modesty, all of us who love you were filled with mourning, dejection, and sighs, seeing the snares of the devil,
who schemes in every way and is preparing to snatch away your hope and salvation in God, and to put to shame the labors you have undertaken for your soul and the orthodox faith.
For it is already clear that if you go to Antioch, you will be unsettled and persuaded by friends and by the man who holds authority there.
Either you will enter into communion with him, or you will be sent away as an enemy—if you are allowed to leave.
Therefore do whatever you can, while we here do what we can, so that you do not offend God, suffer great losses yourself,
and distress us who love you.” When I received this reply, I strengthened my resolve to obey the holy men rather than those who lead people astray.
I implored our Lord and Savior not to neglect me, he who in his mercy had brought me out of darkness and the shadows of death.
But those from Antioch were putting intense pressure on me and striving by every means to take me with them.
Those from Arabia, my relatives and countrymen, also came with them and pressed me.
When they heard, they were delighted and immediately hurried to me, since they were worldly people whose thoughts were occupied with worldly things.
They were setting everything in motion and pressing for my return to Antioch. But I fled to the Lord
and continually fell down before him, while the holy fathers struggled alongside me through their prayers. Then divine providence brought about the following:
They fell ill with a severe and nearly life-threatening disease called hemitritaeus, that is, half-tertian, or tertian fever.
Both Bishop Peter and Solomon the priest were suddenly stricken. When I learned of their illness, I thought it proper and beneficial to visit them,
although I had previously been in great distress, as was evident to everyone. When I went to where they were staying, to a remarkable and conspicuous house,
I saw the bishop lying opposite the doorway, tossing about. When he heard that I was approaching,
although he was burning with fever and tossing about, he sprang up from his bed, crying out, “Welcome, servant of Christ!”
These were his own words, I mean: “Have mercy on me! Have mercy on me! I have sinned against you! I have sinned against you! Whether I live or die rests with you.
I know for certain that I am suffering these things because of you, and that God’s wrath has come upon me. God’s judgment is just! My own destruction and [?] were not enough for me.
But I was calling even you, who stand firm, to share these same views with me and become an apostate.
I beg you: from this day on, we will no longer pressure you. Do as you wish; only pray for me.
For you see our distress and the danger in which we both find ourselves, and that we are on the final stretch.
As for me, I was astonished and bewildered at what was being said, and I asked what had caused these words
and such a change. With much sobbing and tears, he began to recount the whole matter from the very beginning:
what I have recorded about the blessed Panoprepius, the bishop and confessor, who had been his spiritual father and the superior of his monastery—how he had been at the council,
and how, when he saw from the beginning the bishops’ struggle for the truth, and the betrayal and apostasy that followed, he shut himself inside his lodging and pleaded with the Lord;
what assurance and revelation he was granted, and how he came to his city and proclaimed the truth to them
and exposed the apostasy that had taken place; how he remained unyielding to the end, without becoming an apostate, and so ended his life in glory and at a good old age.
Then Petra spoke about himself with shame and tears: how he had been enticed by the desire to become a bishop,
had yielded to Basil the metropolitan, had betrayed the faith, and had become a participant in the council of these apostates.
When I heard these things, I was deeply grieved and reflected on the greatness of God’s mercy toward me in my wretchedness. After the conversation,
I immediately ran to the holy Church of the Resurrection. I waited for a quiet moment and fell down before the altar and the revered Golgotha.
With bitter tears from the depths of my heart, I cried out and said, “Lord, who am I—[?], a stinking dog, a worm, a rebellious house,
a den of robbers, a tomb of [?]—that you have poured out upon me such abundant mercy and so many wonders, which you have multiplied and performed according to your mercy and compassion?
Thus these people, who came for this very purpose, who are eager and devise every possible scheme, who pressure me and urge me to become an apostate
and fall away from hope in you and from a good conscience, have themselves become a source of strength, edification, and warning for me.
What, then, shall I repay the Lord my God for everything you have done for your servant? For this reason I offer you David’s words, saying:
‘I will give abundant thanks to the Lord with my mouth, and praise him in the midst of many, because he has stood at the right hand of the afflicted,
to save him from his persecutors.’” I considered it both very proper and very necessary that these two awe-inspiring and true accounts
should be set before everyone, as on a public monument, for the knowledge of all who fear God and are zealous for the orthodox faith,
so that they may be convinced wholeheartedly and without doubt that a sentence has gone out from heaven above, condemning the Council of Chalcedon and everything done at it,
and all those who share and teach the same views as its members. But since I have mentioned Isauria,
it is fitting that, to confirm what has been said, I should also add this account of the blessed Stephen,
who was the abbot of the monastery called Tagon, which is in Seleucia in Isauria.
He who in his time was the foremost champion of the orthodox faith, and the source of this radiance that has now shone forth, first in Isauria and from there throughout the East.
He who was glorified and brought to perfection in that contest, fought the good fight, and finished his race, and for these things rightly received the crown.
23. The account is as follows. “I was a friend and close companion,” he said, “of Basil,
who was bishop of Seleucia in Isauria. For he had a reputation for preaching well and eloquently.
When the Council of Chalcedon assembled, he too attended it, together with the other bishops from Isauria who were under his authority.

Previously he had been regarded as a zealous and thoroughly orthodox man. But when the denial of the faith that had taken place there became known and was heard about everywhere, everyone was seized with astonishment and amazement.
They would not accept that Basil too had denied the faith and become entangled in the betrayal committed by those others. Above all, I would not, since I had been his friend and admirer.
But when he returned to Isauria and was about to enter the metropolis, many were uncertain and resolved not to enter into communion with him
until they had received complete assurance concerning the truth. I was among them too,” said the blessed Stephen.
“While I was still a layman, I was uncertain and pleaded with God, in faith and with a sincere heart, to make the truth about this matter known to my lowly self.
And immediately, that very night, I seemed to see Basil returning, with all the people running to meet him. They brought him into the church with honor, praise, and acclamation.
As the gathering of the great crowd was about to be complete, he was standing in the sanctuary, with the whole city present, including women and children.
A man entered through the western doors of the church, fearsome in appearance, tall and glorious. He cut through the people and rushed at Basil,
who was standing ready to complete the prayer. He put a finger of his right hand into Basil’s mouth and turned toward his face.
In this way he kept pulling at him and rebuking him, while no one restrained him or dared to make a sound. He took him out of the church, drove him away, and cast him out.”
This was a prophecy of what was to happen under the administration now established by the holy and blessed Severus,
archbishop of the great city of Antioch. For behold, Basil’s name has been silenced and erased from the diptychs,
and he has become rejected by God and by the saints. From this let us take heed: although God was patient, yet now, after so long a time,
behold, this vision has been fulfilled. Nevertheless, ever since the denial of the faith took place at the Council of Chalcedon,
those who arranged it have been cast out and placed under a curse by God and by human beings.
The elder Stephen said, “At that time I was young and a layman, inexperienced in the precise understanding of divine doctrines.
When I saw that everyone was being deceived by him—for he was skillful in speaking, and it seemed that he convinced everyone that he spoke correctly—
while he concealed his shame and wickedness, I too became entangled along with everyone else and entered into communion with him. But now that I have been judged worthy to know the light of truth
and to share in the Eucharist of the orthodox, I have remembered that vision, and from it I have received, to a very great extent, firm assurance.”
24. He also added this concerning him. For he told me, revealing it to me as to a beloved friend, that some time previously one of Christ’s servants
He saw a vision like this. Speaking about my humble self, he said, “I thought I saw a large building shaped like a church.
In it were many thrones, and on the thrones were many bishops. Suddenly you came in”—he was speaking about me.
“When you saw them sitting there, you cried out and said, ‘Look! Deniers of the faith and outcasts!’ You took a whip, drove them away, and threw them out.
And you overturned their thrones.” As Father Stephen related all these things together, he asked to learn from me,
“What, then, does this sign mean?” I said, “God knows. Nevertheless, it is an awesome vision, not an empty one.”
But, as the outcome showed, the vision foretells the present government, through which and by whose hands come the orthodox faith and the rejection and condemnation of the heretical bishops.
25. Hear also another verdict that came from heaven concerning the Council of Chalcedon.
The one who heard it, and who witnessed and proclaimed it, was the blessed Romanus, who is acclaimed everywhere.
He was the abbot and leader of the large monastery opposite the village of Tekoa, which lies about fifteen miles south of Jerusalem.
At that time there were more than six hundred monks in it, shepherded by this holy man and practicing stillness.
For when news spread throughout the East of the denial of the faith and the transgression of Juvenal and those who had assembled at Chalcedon, who were called bishops,
the faithful everywhere were overcome by boundless mourning and deep distress, especially the holy order of monks.
Leaving their monasteries, they hurried to him as to a father of them all, a man clothed in God who stood before God at all times.
I mean the holy Romanus. They begged him, like the prophet Elijah, to show a zeal worthy of the Lord,
and not to disregard the faith being betrayed and the wickedness prevailing. They reminded him of what they had heard from Juvenal, the denier of the faith,
when he was about to leave for the council and solemnly declared to everyone,
“Whoever agrees to this Tome has a share with Simon the Magician and Judas the betrayer, and ought to receive circumcision like the Jews.”
As he was being pressed by the many holy monks and urged to leave his monastery, join them in their zealous struggle, and endure every hardship for the truth,
he persuaded them, saying, “Wait for me a few days. After that, come to me, and whatever the Lord gives me assurance about,
I will do.” He left his monastery and went alone into the wilderness, where he spent ten days and nights prostrate before the Lord.
He wanted God's will and judgment concerning the events at Chalcedon to be revealed to him, because of the conflicting reports circulating everywhere:
some rejected those events and spoke ill of them, while others accepted them. After the ten days had ended,
he heard a voice speaking from heaven: “Go, believe as you were baptized, in the faith of the three hundred and eighteen, and you will be saved.”
Having received complete assurance, he returned to his monastery and disclosed the vision to some chaste men and knowledgeable elders of his monastery.
But they said to him, “Those very men who assembled at Chalcedon were affirming this same faith of the three hundred and eighteen.”
And they follow it, so to speak, deceitfully—that definition of the 318. They placed it at the beginning of their own definition to entice and mislead many.
And again he went into the wilderness alone. While enduring the same hardship and practicing ascetic discipline, he pleaded with the Lord,
to receive complete assurance. And a voice came to him, saying, “Go, follow these men and their teaching, and remain in their tradition:
Peter, archbishop of Alexandria; Gregory of Neocaesarea, the great wonder-worker; Julius of Rome;
Athanasius, Basil, Gregory, John of Constantinople, Cyril, Celestine, and Dioscorus.” And when he had received complete assurance,
he returned joyfully to his monastery. When he told these holy men, he said, he heard from them, “These deniers too appear to follow these men,
while falsely interpreting their teachings and misleading the simple. Therefore you should ask God's mercy for clear and unquestionable assurance
as to whether the Council of Chalcedon reached an evil decision or a good one.” And when he went out into the wilderness and practiced abstinence and strenuous labor,
he prayed with bitter tears and groans, asking the Lord's mercy for a clear and unambiguous answer. And it came to him in this way:
At midday he saw a large scroll descending from heaven. These words were written on it: “Those at Chalcedon have denied the faith. They have transgressed! They have transgressed!
Woe to them, and anathema!” When this blessed man received this assurance from God, his whole being blazed with zeal for the truth and the orthodox faith,
so that he left his monastery and its large community of brothers, despite his advanced old age and bodily weakness,
and went with the holy and zealous monks who had come to him from Arabia and Palestine. At first they planned
to meet the transgressor Juvenal as he returned from that council of wrongdoers with great pomp and honor bestowed by the emperor,
and to try, through counsel, persuasive speech, and gentle words, to turn him from his evil purpose
and bring him back to correct doctrine. But when they found him unwilling to be persuaded, relying on a mortal emperor,
and determined to please him rather than God, the whole assembly of holy men anathematized him to his face and returned to Jerusalem.
There gathered there, so to speak, all the holy monks and laypeople from every city, together with the orthodox bishops
who had remained behind and had not gone up to the council. First, by a written anathema, they cast down and rejected the wretched Juvenal and publicly proclaimed it.
After this, by a common vote, they elected as bishop a zealous and holy man adorned with every apostolic virtue—
I mean the blessed Theodosius, a second James and brother of our Lord. They established him as leader, guide, and shepherd in the holy city itself.
Through his hands and by him, bishops were appointed in all the cities. The people hastened with great eagerness, jointly choosing and presenting
a man who pleased everyone and was adorned with right faith and blameless conduct. But if anyone does not accept what has been said,
such a person may take into his hands the letter that Abba Romanus wrote to them, addressed to Empress Eudocia,
while he was in Antioch, where he had been driven into exile by the wicked tyrant Marcian. From it he will be fully assured of the whole truth.
Concerning this account that has been set down: it is entirely full of wisdom and instruction. For what happened then did not happen only because of these things,
but also as a statement of the precision of the doctrines of truth and of the faith that is uncorrupted and free from error.
For everyone who is willing and understands, it is sufficient as an unquestionable demonstration and confirmation of the truth, and as a rebuke to the transgression at Chalcedon.
26. There was a priest named Aphlanus in Caesarea who used to gather God's church of the orthodox there. He was a man humble and holy in every way.
He was honored and respected by everyone. He suffered greatly and showed zeal for the true faith. He used to tell this story:
While the blessed confessor Timothy, the archbishop, was still in exile in Cherson,
he went to visit him and to receive his blessing. But when he saw that he had a malignant ulcer on his foot,
which physicians call “cacoethes,” meaning “of a bad kind,” and which was causing decay, he said, “I reproached his attendants,
as though they were neglecting the old man's health. But they reassured me, saying,
‘Many times we have pleaded and asked him to let us clean the ulcer and apply the appropriate treatment, but we have not been able to persuade him.
But now, my lord, the love of God within you has brought you here, and you would do well to do what you can too.’
So, feeling compassion for the old man myself and burning with love, I clasped the holy man's feet when the brothers were not nearby,
so that I would not be thought to have done this at their suggestion. I pleaded with him, saying, ‘Have mercy on me,
and grant me what I ask of you.’ But the holy man said, ‘Get up. We will do what you ask, if it is possible.’
But I remained lying face down and kept saying, ‘I will not get up unless you grant me this favor.’
But the holy man said, ‘Do not argue. I have already said that I will do what is possible and pleasing to God.’
When I got up, I begged him to consent and allow me to do, with care, whatever was possible and beneficial
for the ulcer on his foot. But he said to me, ‘Stay now, sit down, and listen. Do not be argumentative.’
Putting his finger on his eye, he said to me, ‘Look: what do you see here? Do you not see something like a thick spot in the pupil of my eye?’
I said, ‘Yes.’ And he said to me, ‘Even if I am being foolish, nevertheless, so that you may be persuaded and stop pressing me,
I must tell you how this happened to me. Once, when I had risen early and was keeping vigil
and completing a short service, suddenly someone came, fearsome and terrifying, black and sooty. His appearance was
like the prophet Job's portrayal of Satan. He broke through the wall and came in, holding a large document in his hand.
Stretching out his right hand and shaking it at the same time, he cried out, “Look! Here is the only one who stands against my will!
Here is the one who will not submit to me! Take this and sign it, even now!” He shook, pressed me urgently, and raged with threats, imagining that he could frighten me with his voice.’
But when I had received courage from the Lord and been strengthened, I said to him, “What you say will not happen, nor will I do your will.
I will not fight against God and become a rebel like you. I know your weakness. You do not frighten me or terrify me with your threats and your ravings.”
At these words he became furious and seethed with rage. Indeed, like a serpent or a dragon, he was filled with bitter gall. As I said, he was holding that scroll in his right hand.
He raised it and struck me angrily on my eye. He caused me such bitter pain that I thought my eye had been gouged out and had fallen out.
But, with God’s help, this had not happened. When the brothers came in to see me in the morning, they saw something like a lump of blood and flesh
that was hanging loose and coming down from my eye. For the most part, the whole eye seemed to have been destroyed, and nothing remained in it
of its former proper appearance. They wept and mourned, and begged me to let them use poultices
and the usual remedies that could heal such injuries. For they often thought that an accident like this had occurred from a discharge [?] or some similar cause.
I would not let them, saying, “I know where this has come from. So do not argue or trouble me.
For I have only one physician: the one in heaven.” As I continued patiently, throwing myself down before the Lord and asking for his mercy,
help came to me from him. For our God Jesus Christ himself appeared to me, laid his undefiled hands on my eyes, and healed me.
He gave me my sight and left me this little scar as an unforgettable reminder, and as a reason to give thanks for his gracious care.
Now I know for certain that the one who brought that trial and injury upon me has also now, with our Lord’s permission, brought this ulcer upon my foot.
Just as I then trusted in the Lord, and he healed me when I pleaded with him, so now too I believe without doubt
that his care will soon come to me. So I beg your chastity to be quiet and stop pressing me about this.” The same account.
I also heard it from many others who knew Archbishop Timothy well through personal experience and association with him.
And again, I heard it from one of his cell companions, who had gathered around him there in Cherson and served him in exile.
Having learned these things by experience, the blessed Timothy rightly and frequently calls the council of Chalcedon demonic in his letters and his other writings,
since it was assembled and brought about by the devil himself, and is the forerunner of the Antichrist.
It is that very rebellion which the apostle Paul mentioned when he wrote to the Thessalonians.
27. A soldier named Zeno, the chief officer of the Dacian regiment stationed in Alexandria, was sent to Palestine by Cosmas the chamberlain
to guard Abba Peter, our bishop, and Abba Isaiah, the solitary who lived in seclusion, until his arrival.
He was expecting to take them to Emperor Zeno, for this was what he had been ordered to do.
When he came to Palestine, he told the blessed man the following story in our presence: “A certain Peter, who was a member of the imperial guard,
once told me this: ‘I was a great admirer of Nestorius, and I used to praise the council of Chalcedon and Emperor Marcian.’
Many times I stood against those who accused them. Then one night I saw someone who said to me, “How long will you go astray?
Do you not want to hold firmly to the truth? Come, then, and I will show you among whom Emperor Theodosius is, and among whom Marcian is.”
He showed me the blessed Theodosius in a place filled with unapproachable light, in indescribable glory, shining more brightly than the sun.
He brought me to another place, filled with smoke, gloom, and darkness, and said to me, “Do you see Marcian being tormented there?”
I said, “I cannot see anyone.” He looked up to heaven and said, “Lord, let the gloom clear a little, so that he may see and believe.”
Then I saw Marcian hanging from iron hooks in the midst of the fire, being tormented. In this way I was convinced and became orthodox.
28. Cyriacus and Julius, chaste monks, Cypriots by birth and worthy of belief,
used to tell the blessed Abba Peter what they knew with certainty and had become convinced of through experience:
There is a martyr’s shrine in Cyprus belonging to a certain martyr whose name I do not now remember. Along with his other miraculous deeds, he had this gracious gift:
If someone promised to offer a sheep or a dove there, or one of the other things customarily offered in this way—
as also happens at many other martyrs’ shrines—he would send it off from his house, and it would go on its own.
It would be found in the martyr’s shrine, though no one had guided it, and none of those who encountered it dared to touch it.
When the bishops returned from the Council of Chalcedon and sought to mislead simple people, as though nothing evil had happened, this holy martyr
would appear openly on the roads to those who were coming to his church as usual, bearing witness to them and saying,
“I am so-and-so, the one you are going to visit. Do not go there,
and do not share in communion with the deniers. For this reason I have withdrawn from there and no longer appear there.”
29. This is also similar to what happened at Sebaste in Palestine, where the whole body of John the Baptist lies.
At the time of the Council of Chalcedon, the holy and blessed Constantine was the caretaker of that place.
He was continually delighted by the sight of the Baptist. For there was a separate chamber, an exedra belonging to the martyr’s shrine,
adorned with railings, in which there were two coffins covered with gold and silver, with lamps burning perpetually before them.
One belonged to Saint John the Baptist and one to the prophet Elisha. A throne had been placed and prepared in that place,
on which no one ever sat. Now, whenever the blessed Constantine rose each night for the vigil,
he would first enter that exedra. After greeting those coffins, he would tend the lamps
and carefully arrange that throne. The blessed priest Elatus, whom we mentioned earlier, told us these things about him.
He was the one who gathered together the orthodox church of God in Caesarea, and who, while staying with Saint Constantine,
His disciple said, “When I saw how he cared for his throne every day, I fell down before him and begged him to tell me the reason
why he took such care of the throne when no one sat on it. At first he was reluctant to speak.
But when he saw that I persisted in faith, he said, ‘Almost every night, when I first open the door and enter,
I find the holy Baptist on the throne.’ Now the blessed Constantine had a close relationship with Saint John.
When persecution arose, and the bishops appointed by the blessed Archbishop Theodosius were expelled by Marcian,
he was troubled in his thoughts by two alternatives: either, by fleeing from the Eucharist of the deniers, he would be deprived of companionship with the holy Baptist,
or, by remaining, he would become a wrongdoer. He begged the holy forerunner of Christ to enlighten his mind and reveal to him what was pleasing to God.
He saw the saint, who said to him, ‘Priest, do not destroy your soul on my account and deny your faith. Instead, leave and keep your faith without transgression.
Wherever you go, I am with you.’ So he left without stain and, while living away from his homeland, was preserved in a holy life
and in the orthodox faith until the end. He fought the good fight and won the crown of confessing the faith.
30. The God-fearing priest Zosimus, a stranger and a chaste man, was also found worthy of such assurance and a vision.
He had been found worthy to live with the blessed Abba Peter, and until the end he kept the orthodox faith without transgression,
and was himself preserved by it. While he was living in solitude at Raithu and Mount Sinai, he was in communion with orthodox fathers.
He left these places, as he himself told me, and came to Jerusalem. Having grown to love the way of life in these holy places,
he went around looking for a place suitable for solitude. When he came to Bethel, where the patriarch Jacob saw the ladder,
the caretaker of that place became fond of him and urged him very strongly to remain there,
promising to provide him with suitable comforts. He openly told him that he could not do this, because he was fleeing from the Eucharist of those deniers at Chalcedon.
The man again promised him, saying that he would not subject him to any pressure at all over this matter. He said, ‘Only stay here
and chant the psalms with me, and look after this place.’ When his mind inclined toward this proposal,
he saw the patriarch Jacob at night: a gray-haired man, dignified and gaunt, wrapped in a cloak and holding a staff. He was walking about the place in this manner, and approached him and said,
‘How is it that, although you are orthodox and share communion with the orthodox, you wish to settle here? Do not transgress against your faith on my account.
Instead, take care and flee from communion with the deniers. You will lack none of the good things, neither a place to live nor the necessities of life.’
So he fled and was preserved unwavering until the end, in holy conduct and in the orthodox faith.
31. The blessed Abba Peter, the bishop, used to tell us about one of the holy men who was called Heliodorus the Shepherd.
He left the world and came to the mountaintops and the wooded depths of the Taurus Mountains in Cilicia.
He chose to live among wild animals for many years, dwelling there in forgetfulness of human beings.
For unprepared food he used shoots from trees and wild roots. His hair therefore served him in place of a ragged garment, in winter and summer.
Now hunters of deer and wild animals came, as they usually did, to those places.
They saw the holy man from a distance and thought he was an unfamiliar animal because of his wild appearance.
They set a trap and caught him, after many years of such ascetic living.
Once he had become known in this way, he could no longer follow the practices of self-emptying that accord with the cross.
He was persuaded—or rather compelled—by the inhabitants of those places to return to the world. He settled in a monastery and became the father of its monks.
When he was about to die, he called his disciples and said to them, “After twenty-four years,
the bishops will renounce the faith. But when you see the beginning of this upheaval, flee to Egypt.
For from there a remnant of the orthodox will be preserved.” And that is what they did in Palestine. As our blessed father used to say, he went to Egypt
and found one of his disciples still alive and living quietly there, an old and holy man. I heard these things from him and was convinced.
32. The blessed Abba Peter also said that he knew one of the holy men who, when the blessed and orthodox Emperor Theodosius died,
was sitting in his cell and heard a voice from heaven saying, “Look, heaven is shaking and is about to fall and devastate the earth,
yet no one grieves. For the great orthodox Emperor Theodosius has died.”
33. Abba also used to tell us about a certain Comatinus, one of the distinguished men of Alexandria, who regularly came to him
and received communion from him. He used to tell him, “At the time when the wicked Nestorius was in exile in Thebes,
I was sent by the count to distribute pay to the soldiers there. Out of necessity I spent time in his company, and I heard many of his blasphemies.
While I was in his company, someone came announcing his recall and saying that an imperial courier who was to fetch him would arrive immediately.
Elated in his mind and filled with joy, that vile man said, ‘What? Was I wrong, then, to say that Christ is not God
and that Mary is not the Mother of God?’ As he spoke, his tongue came loose and hung far out of his mouth. And so he died while chewing it,
one day before the arrival of the imperial courier who had been sent for this purpose.” And as Abba Theodore the monk used to relate and affirm—
the man who later became a bishop—when he went to that place, he learned through firsthand experience and confirmed that not even the earth accepted his corpse after his death.
Instead, it cast him out three times, so that the inhabitants there were compelled to wrap him in a basket
and hang him on a wall. The blessed Timothy included an account of this
in the Ecclesiastical History that he wrote. I hope, if our Lord grants it, to include that account among the things written here.
34. Potamon, one of those holy monks of old who were in Scetis, left there and was living in a cell in Egypt at that time.
At that same time our father, having departed from Palestine, was staying in Egypt. He used to say about him
that he had such a gift of power over demons that he would merely sprinkle water in the name of Christ on those who were afflicted,
and in this way drive out the demons. When he heard about the blessed man called Spelarius, he went to receive his blessing, concealing his identity so that no one would know who he was
or where he came from. Proterius was then living in Alexandria and was inflicting many hardships on the saints.
But Potamon, knowing through the Spirit who the father was, said this to him as soon as he entered: “Do not be distressed, Father Peter the bishop; do not be distressed.
For God will soon exact vengeance. Look, the church of God is pleading on your behalf, you chief priests.
And this man who sleeps with males, this murderer, will be killed.” He was speaking about Proterius. Three days later Proterius was killed.
35. There was a deacon named Basil, an Antiochene by birth, who was one of the well-known clergy.
He had been a guide to salvation for Father Peter when he was a boy and was in the imperial city.
He kindled in him the fire and life of monasticism. That blessed man used to say about him that he had left the world, taken up Christ’s cross, and followed him.
For thirty-five years he lived alone in silence in the desert of the Thebaid. Finally he heard a voice from heaven saying to him, “Basil,
go to the inhabited world and fight for the faith, for bishops and kings are about to deny the only-begotten Son of God.”
When he came to the region of Lycia, he found an inaccessible place on a cliff by the sea. He lived there for twelve years,
following the same way of life and ascetic discipline as the previously mentioned Father Heliodorus, who had been a shepherd.
When a ship anchored there, the sailors went ashore to obtain what they needed and found him. They made him known to the inhabitants there.
Once he had become known in this way, the people of that region persuaded him to come to the inhabited parts of Lycia.
When he came, he established two communities of holy monastics, one for men and the other for women.
In those days the wicked Nestorius was bishop of Constantinople and was proclaiming his blasphemies.
Again he heard a voice from heaven saying to him, “Basil, make haste and go to Constantinople.
Rebuke the wicked Nestorius, who blasphemes and has denied faith in me.” Without delay, he went to Constantinople.
When he entered the church and found the wicked Nestorius standing on the platform and preaching, he rebuked him before all the people, saying,
“Correct yourself, bishop! You are teaching wrongly. Why are you overturning and twisting the teachings of the fathers?”
When Nestorius persisted in his teaching, Basil cried out, “A curse on you, Nestorius, and on your wickedness!”
After the assembly had dispersed, Nestorius summoned him, and Basil exposed his wickedness in the presence of the bishops who were there.
Finally, he approached Emperor Theodosius as he was passing through the marketplace and said to him in a loud voice, “Emperor, why, although you have been baptized into the Trinity,
do you not acknowledge the Trinity? For the things Nestorius teaches are contrary to the Trinity.”
He was seized by Flavian the Thracian, who was then a magister and a tyrant.
He suffered greatly at his hands, was scourged and beaten, and became hated by everyone. Flavian sentenced him to exile. While he was being paraded through the city,
the people snatched him away and brought him into the church of Saint Euphemia. He lived there for some time, pleading with the Lord who had sent him,
imploring him and asking him not to remain indifferent to the end while the wicked Nestorius acted arrogantly against the worship of God. While he was occupied with these things,
the following providential event occurred: when the blessed Emperor Theodosius went out into the marketplace, a roof tile fell from above and struck his head.
It nearly brought him into danger of death. When he recovered beyond all expectation, he was filled with great fear and trembling.
At night he saw someone who said to him, “You have suffered this because of Basil, the servant of God, because you do not listen to him as he struggles for the worship of God.”
Immediately he sent for the holy man and had him brought. Once he had some relief, he appealed to him, seeking to learn from him what would satisfy him, so that he could do it.
But he said, “I do not seek what satisfies me, but what pleases God and strengthens his churches.
Order a council to be held so that Nestorius’s blasphemies against God may be exposed, and let him be deposed and cast out. For this is the will of God.”
The emperor was persuaded without delay. He ordered a council to be held at Ephesus, and Nestorius to be deposed and sent into exile.
36. Abba Peter the bishop used to tell us that the wife of Damarius, who was praetorian prefect,
was the blessed Helena, a holy woman who gave alms and loved Christ in everything. [?] years before Nestorius became bishop,
an angel appeared to her and said, “Helena, Helena, three years from now so-and-so is going to take his seat as bishop in Constantinople.
See that you guard yourself and do not receive Communion from him.” After three years, Nestorius became bishop.
She would never agree to receive him in her house, although he came to see her many times, nor would she receive the holy mysteries from him.
But when she heard his blasphemies and was set ablaze with divine zeal, she came to the church, wanting to be certain of the truth.
