It happened that on that very day, while he was preaching, the blessed Basil, the deacon of Antioch whom we mentioned earlier, came and rebuked him.
From above, in the upper galleries, she cried out in a loud voice and pronounced an anathema against him, saying, “Anathema to you, Antichrist!”
She remembered the dream she had seen about so-and-so, for that dream had pointed to the heretics who teach two natures. And since this has been mentioned,
it is fitting that we should also marvel at what finally happened to Nestorius in exile, confirming the truth of the blessed Helena’s dream.
For he was sent into exile at the Oasis, was captured by the barbarians called the Mazices, became a prisoner, and was released.
He was no longer allowed to remain in the Oasis itself, but instead in the city called Panopolis, which was named after that creature of two natures.
He was kept there until his end, at the time we have mentioned. Under the blow of God's wrath, he received his sentence—or rather, he was struck down and died.
To confirm this, I considered it necessary to take that portion of the history written about this matter by the blessed Timothy, the chief bishop,

and place it here in this account.
From Saint Timothy, Archbishop of Alexandria: from the history he wrote while he was in Gangra.
At that time, by God's permission and will, it happened because of our many sins that our blessed emperor Theodosius passed away,
one year after the second council was held at Ephesus. But the man who assumed imperial power after him did not imitate his burning zeal for the faith.
Consequently, all the affairs [?] of the church were thrown into confusion, contrary to the law against heretics
that had been issued by the blessed Theodosius, who is worthy of remembrance. For from that time until now, those who fear God have been persecuted.
Every blasphemous and insolent tongue gained freedom to speak against Christ. For immediately after Marcian became emperor,
he sent a tribune of the notaries to Egypt to summon the wicked Nestorius and a certain Dorotheus, who had been a bishop.
This man had gone into exile with Nestorius of his own accord and willingly. According to what some people reported,
this Dorotheus was a very close acquaintance and friend of the man who had then become emperor.
When the tribune who had been sent reached the Thebaid—as eventually became known to many, for this was not done publicly—
he found Nestorius in the place called Panopolis, a city in the Thebaid, where he was being held in a fortress.
He was being wasted by a terrible illness. It had happened that Nestorius had been captured by barbarians in the Oasis,
where he had been living in exile by order of the blessed emperor Theodosius, and had been sold by those barbarians to people of that same city, Panopolis.
When Count Andrew, who was then in the Thebaid, learned of this, while Emperor Theodosius was still alive,
he sent word to Nestorius after he had been sold, advising him to remain quietly in that fortress and not to act or speak insolently.
When the man sent by the emperor found Nestorius ill in the city of Panopolis, as mentioned above, together with Dorotheus,
he told them what he had been ordered to do. Because of the Egyptians, he informed them somewhat secretly,
so that no plot would be made against those who had been summoned. But Dorotheus persuaded him to wait a little because of Nestorius's weakness.
Day by day Nestorius grew worse and worse. While that tribune was there, his tongue came loose and protruded from his mouth,
and his voice became unintelligible. Every day his tongue continued to grow slack and come apart, until he became a horrifying and distressing sight,
as the tribune who had been sent later confirmed to many, calling God to witness what he said.
For he related that from all those cities, so to speak, that lay in the neighborhood of the city of Panopolis,
he diligently brought skilled physicians. But they could do nothing to help the sick man. For, he said, it was God who had struck him.
The earthquake made his death known to many through reports of it, and through the doctors’ contempt. And when Nestorius himself died,
Dorotheus buried him in a certain place, with the tribune who had been sent there present with him. After his death, Apion, the tribune, returned to the imperial court.
37. I also heard the following account from Father while I was living with him in Arca, a city of Phoenicia. He said:
“While I was still living in the world and residing in the palace at Constantinople, I watched over myself carefully and lived ascetically.
Questions arose in my mind about the mystery of the Holy Trinity: how, although we confess one God,
we believe in a Trinity equal in essence, eternal and without beginning, and whether the one who became flesh for our sake is one of the Trinity.”
He said that in a vision he saw the holy apostle Peter, who took him and brought him to a high place, and had him stand before him as in ordinary life.
He showed him in heaven a great, unapproachable and incomprehensible light, which had a circular shape like the sun, and said to him, “Here is the Father.”
Immediately there was another [?], adjoining the first and resembling it in every respect. In its center was our Lord, as the Nazarene is depicted. Again he said to him, “Here is the Son.”
Alongside it was a third light, resembling the first two in every respect, and Saint Peter said to him, “Here is the Holy Spirit. One essence,
one nature, one glory, one power, one light, one Godhead, three persons.” But although all three were unapproachable,
only the middle one appeared to have the visible form of the man from Nazareth, to show that the one who was crucified is one of the Holy Trinity,
and not someone else—far be it! The other two were simply light, unapproachable, without form, incomprehensible and beyond understanding.
38. There was a certain Anianus, a lawyer, who was chaste, modest and orthodox, just as his father also was.
While staying in Alexandria, he was found worthy to receive baptism from our Father. Afterward he went to Cilicia.
When he settled in the imperial city, he married a modest woman, adorned with the other virtues, but not orthodox: she was in communion with the adherents of two natures.
Although he often urged her to join the orthodox, she remained unpersuaded. He was therefore moved by divine zeal
and holy love to write repeatedly to our blessed Father, who was in Palestine—for it was from him alone that he received communion—
asking him to pray to God for his wife, that God would draw her away from communion with the adherents of two natures. When the holy man prayed earnestly,
the following providential event occurred. The blessed woman fell seriously ill, so that the doctors gave up all hope for her.
When she was close to death, she saw this vision: angels carried her to a gloomy place, full of darkness and stench.
There were the sounds of people weeping, with no rest or comfort at all. Then, from there,
the angels took her and brought her to another place, full of light, glory and indescribable joy.
There she saw a gathering of saints, dressed in shining garments and praising God.
Then the angels said to her, “Look, these are the people with whom your husband is in communion.”
These others, however, are those who are in communion with the bishops who accept the Council of Chalcedon.
If, then, you wish to be in communion with these people, we will plead with our Lord on your behalf to grant you one more year of life.
Rise, then, and live in peace with your husband, sharing his faith. And in communion with him, keep yourself from every sin and from negligence.
When the year is over, we will come and take you and place you in this place.” And when she had recovered from her weakness,
she immediately called her husband, who was sitting in mourning with many others in another room, dressed in black.
He rose without delay, so that those who were near him thought that she had died. But he came to her.
When he found that she had revived, he sent everyone outside and learned from her what God had providentially done for her.
Then she plainly related everything about the vision. She cried out to him, saying, “My recovery depends on you.
If you want me to live and be with you, give me some of the holy Eucharist of the orthodox, from the place where you receive communion.”
Convinced that this was God's will, he noted the day on which she had seen the vision. He also had some of the Eucharist,
which was sent to him every year by Abba Peter the bishop. Having believed her and put his trust in her, he first required a declaration from her.
He gave her some of the saving mysteries. She rose and lived a chaste and virtuous life in orthodoxy and in complete uprightness.
At the very end of the year she died. Anianus the lawyer related these wonders to those accompanying the abbot and bishop Abba John,
and Abba Julian the priest, and Abba Andrew and Paul, and Abba Theodore and their entire company, when they had been summoned by Emperor Zeno and were traveling to Constantinople.
39. Similar to this story is the account of the blessed Claudian, who was administrator of all the property of the church of the city of Eleutheropolis.
He was in communion with the bishops, but he had faith in and love for the blessed Abba Romanus, and he gave many generous alms to his monastery,
both while Romanus was alive and after his death. For this man too became ill, and when he was near his end, he was granted a vision
and an assurance similar to that one. Immediately, without delay, he ordered his household at night, when no one could see,
to take him and carry him to the monastery of Abba Romanus, which was five miles away.
When he arrived there, he made his confession to the holy fathers and abbots who were with Abba Leontius, and acknowledged and related to them the events of the vision.
He earnestly implored and pleaded with tears and sobs that he might be deemed worthy not only to receive the Eucharist of the orthodox but also to receive the monastic habit.
After living for only three days in complete joy and gladness, he died and was buried with the priests.
The cause of this wondrous salvation for him was almsgiving, which can accomplish all things.
40. The blessed Boniface, the Roman priest, was so fervently zealous against the Council of Chalcedon that he would not receive any of its adherents even for ordinary conversation,
not even a layman, or ever associate with him, unless he first anathematized the Council of Chalcedon.
Even if someone met him on the road, and especially because he had seen a vision like this when the persecution took place.
He said that he seemed to see a dead man lying on a bier before the Holy Resurrection, badly decomposed, with the air filled by his stench.
Suddenly this man came to life and was about to reign. He held a book in his hand, and as he gave it to the priest Boniface, he said:
“Take this book from me.” On the outside it was splendidly decorated, but when he received it from him and opened it, he found it full of soot inside.
The meaning of this was that Nestorius, although dead, had come to life through Juvenal,
who had become the heir to his empty doctrine. The blessed Abba Peter also used to say that the wretched Juvenal had so filled the church with negligent men
that something like this could happen in his days. At that time Abba Peter himself was living quietly in the Holy City.
41. A certain dissolute deacon, while awaiting his day of service at the Holy Resurrection and the shrine of the Holy Martyrs, had intercourse with a woman.
He went inside to sleep, as usual, in the upper room at the holy place of Golgotha, on a bed that had been made up because it was summer.
While the doors were shut, a voice rang out: “Oh, with how much uncleanness Juvenal has filled my house! They have defiled it. Throw this vile fellow outside!”
In the morning, while the doors were still shut, he was found in the street before the shrine of the Holy Martyrs, asleep on his bed and being mocked.
Many people came running, and he woke up, became aware of his disgrace, and was stricken with remorse. With tears he told everyone his sin.
Fear and trembling seized everyone because of what had happened. So Juvenal, they said, was ashamed and removed him from service.

For this reason Abba used to say of the blessed deacon Gerontius, who then belonged to the monastery of the blessed Melania, that whenever he was to perform the evening service there, he would fast for two days at a time.
42. Before the Council of Chalcedon, Juvenal himself wanted
to ordain the blessed Abba, who was living quietly in the Holy City in his cell beside the tower of the patriarch David.
But the blessed man knew about this, so he kept watch over himself and did not go anywhere. When an assembly was held at Holy Zion,
Juvenal sent men to seize him from his nearby cell and bring him to him. As those who had been [?] were about to approach his cell,
he heard a voice saying to him: “Get up and escape through this little door, because some men have been sent after you by Juvenal
to take you by force so that he can ordain you.” Immediately he got up and threw himself down from a high roof.
With the Lord helping and protecting him, he landed upright on his feet when he fell.
In this way he got away and escaped from their hands. From that day onward he refused to worship together with that impious man.
43. A certain woman in the region of Ashkelon, the blessed Mica, lived to be a hundred years old,
leading a life of ascetic discipline, complete chastity, and fear of God. She had experience of the grace of God,
and through it she had received full assurance concerning the persecution that took place at the Council of Chalcedon. She exposed it before everyone's eyes.
She used to call those who had not entered into communion with it blessed, and she encouraged them. She saw Satan openly threatening her with death and [?] to her:
“Why do you dare to make people stumble over the great council and to slander it?”
He threw her, an elderly woman, from the bench on which she was lying, and persisted for a long time in fighting with her,
until she was strengthened in faith, picked up some dust, and threw it at him in the name of the Lord. In this way she drove him away, so that he no longer dared to approach her.
Abba Theodore the priest told us this. He had conversed with her on several occasions and had benefited from her virtue and holiness.
44. The blessed Urbicia, the deaconess, was the daughter of one of the bishops of Crete.
When her father died, she loved Christ and renounced the world together with her brother, the blessed Euphrasius. She undertook a complete renunciation of the world—
I mean living in a foreign land—when she left her city and came to the holy city with her brother.
They bought a monastery near the holy place of the Ascension and lived there in solitude, practicing asceticism well.
They persevered in the service of God. After some time, it happened that the holy bishop Epiphanius of Pamphylia,
after the revocation of the Encyclical, because he would not agree with the other bishops in revoking it,
was driven from his church in Pamphylia and went into exile. He came to the holy city and was received by them, and with them he lived in solitude and asceticism,
as an example, a source of strength, and an encouragement to everyone. But the devil, envying them, stirred up the following persecution against them.
The leader of Jerusalem at that time sent the archdeacon of the Church of the Ascension, along with some other men, to rebuke them.
When he came to them and saw their virtue, since he was close to them,
he advised them, saying, “Enter into communion with the bishop, and you will have your little monastery, peace, and his friendship.” But the blessed woman said,
“How can we break the promise we made to Christ and enter into communion with the Council of Chalcedon?”
He said, “Enter into communion at my own risk, and this will not be a sin for you.” The blessed woman turned to him
and said, “Tell me, my lord father, how much is this risk of yours worth, that I should sell the salvation of my soul for such a thing?
“Listen, then: even if the saints Enoch, Noah, and Daniel were to consent and advise me to enter into communion with you,
and even if a voice came from heaven above, telling me to obey you and enter into communion with you,
I would never consent to do this, unless my own father Timothy, the holy monk,
who handed down the orthodox faith to me in Crete, should himself come back to life, come here, and release me from the condemnation and anathema that he laid upon me.
“Let anyone who has ears to hear listen.” Because they were counted worthy to suffer insult and persecution for Christ together with Saint Epiphanius,
and to have their monastery taken from them, along with the servant who was in it, and to win the crown of confessing the faith, they went to Alexandria.
They were received with honor by the orthodox clergy there, as well as by the monks and laypeople. In many ways they glorified God and were glorified by him.
Finally they returned to Maiuma near Gaza. There they finished the race of their confession of faith and reached their end.
Now she was a blessed, God-clothed woman and a prophetess, filled with all the grace of the Holy Spirit.
She is dead in body but alive in spirit. And, to speak the truth, having chosen the good portion for herself, she has her dwelling in heaven.
45. The blessed father used to tell us about two holy, elderly monks from Cilicia, Torquatus and Hermogenes, who went up to Constantinople [?] in his time and told him
that Theodore, that wicked heretic, the bishop of Mopsuestia, who taught two natures and was Nestorius’s teacher along with Diodore, spoke so outrageously against God
that he sought, as far as he could, to do away with the letters found in the Acts of the Apostles and the Gospel of John.
“When we went in to him and reproached him,” they said, “he rebuked us, saying that it was not for monks to investigate such matters.
And so he drove us away with insults. Three days later, he became possessed by a demon and died while devouring himself.”
After the Encyclical, many holy monks everywhere, through the power and grace of Christ,
refused to agree to its reversal. Instead, aflame with divine zeal, they remained steadfast in the true faith and confession.
46. A demonstration of this kind took place in Pamphylia. Some monks who were in agreement with those bishops who taught two natures,
while cutting wood in the forests, entered into a discussion with orthodox monks, examining and debating the faith.
Both sides agreed to conduct a trial by fire and to receive their verdict from it.
They threw into the blazing fire the Encyclical of the true faith and the statement of faith of the council at Chalcedon, together with Leo’s Tome.
They waited to receive God’s judgment. Immediately, without delay, when the Definition and Leo’s Tome came into contact with the fire,
they became ashes and dust at once. But that divine Encyclical was preserved without blemish or damage in the midst of the fire.
Because of this, those who shared communion with the deniers repented and withdrew from error. Taking up zeal for the fear of God, they became orthodox.
47. If anyone does not believe this miracle, to which God is witness, here is a similar event that took place.
As the blessed Basilides, that outstanding monk, told us, something like this happened in a village near Ptolemais,
where the monastery of Abba Claudian is situated. During that time of denial, he was a zealous champion, a contender, and a leader in the struggle for the orthodox faith.
What happened was this. The priest of that village was disputing with one of its inhabitants, a layman,
who was orthodox and zealous for the faith. He disputed with him about the faith and pressured him either to share communion with him or to leave the village.
While all the villagers were standing beside him, that priest called out to the orthodox man, saying,
“Do you want us to put to the test who believes rightly? Let us light a fire, and let you and me put our right hands into the fire.”
And the one whose hand is preserved unharmed clearly possesses the orthodox faith. But the layman was saying:
“I am a layman and a sinner, while you are a priest. How can I submit to judgment with you in this matter?”
The villagers who were standing there cheered and clapped their hands at this proposal, and they pressed for it to be carried out.
The orthodox man agreed. Immediately a large quantity of wood was gathered, and a brazier was raised up.
The villagers bound the hands of both men with forked branches, brought them close to the fire, and thrust them into it.
The priest’s hand was immediately burned all over, without delay. But the hand of the faithful orthodox layman remained unharmed.
The blessed monk Basilides assured us of this, saying, “At that time I was an oil seller.
While selling oil in those places, I was granted the privilege of conversing with that confessor. I rejoiced with him, took comfort, and was strengthened.”
48. Hear also of a miracle like this one, which happened in a village on an estate called Aphta. Beside it is also the monastery of Saint Salonas, the father of the monks.
There lived there a certain monk named Epiphanius, who was chaste, humble, and richly endowed with kindness. He held to the orthodox faith together with his community,
having received it from the holy fathers and orthodox monks—I mean the blessed Tatian and Maron, who were his relatives.
But the common enemy, the deviser of schemes, envied their salvation and stirred up against them the village priest, a powerful and quarrelsome man.
When he saw that this man alone had separated himself from his church and would not share communion with him or with the villagers—
indeed, the villagers were inciting him against the man—he summoned him and threatened him with beatings, humiliation, and expulsion, saying that on the following day,
if he did not come forward and share communion with him, he would suffer these things. But the poor orthodox man said to him, “It is impossible for me to betray my faith,
which I received from the holy fathers.” When he was released, he prepared to flee and to offer his exile to God,
laying before God the distress he was in and the persecution he endured for his name. The next day, although the priest was healthy and had nothing wrong with him, he died.
Thus all the inhabitants of the village were filled with fear and astonishment at what had happened, and they left the orthodox Epiphanius alone

and no longer harassed him. Having received the crown of noble zeal from the righteous Judge, he was granted the privilege of being cared for in his illness in the communal monastery of our holy and blessed father Isaiah,
where he had been accustomed to partake of the mysteries. When his life ended there, he was buried in the church among the saints, in a tomb of his own.
49. When Abba had left Maiuma after the visitation and was in Alexandria,
he was welcomed there by one of those who loved strangers and the saints, and he remained unknown to many.
Abba Pior, the father of the monks, a prophetic man renowned everywhere, heard a voice saying to him, “Get up and travel to the city of Alexandria.
Go in to Bishop Peter, the confessor who has been driven out and is hiding there. Comfort and strengthen him, and take comfort in one another.”
When Abba Pior said, “Who will show me the place where he is?” the voice said to him, “Set out on the road, and do not worry.”
He got up during the night and came to the city. As he entered the gate, he saw a pillar of fire guiding him, not only through the street but as far as the courtyard,
and up the staircase itself, through its many stories, until he reached the place where Saint Peter was.
Abba Pior went up and knocked at the door. The blessed man was afraid to open it for him, because he did not know who he was. Abba Pior said, “Do not be afraid, Abba Peter.
It is I, poor Pior. The Lord has sent me to you.” So he opened the door and welcomed the holy man. They rejoiced together and were greatly comforted.
Now it happened that the master of the house had a little baby who had not yet been baptized, and he begged the father to baptize him.
The blessed man hesitated, because he had no suitable place, and those who ought to assist him in the service were not nearby.
The man persisted, pressing him and pleading with him, until the blessed man was forced to shut the door and refuse to open it.
God knows how, when the door was opened, that infant was found before the holy man, crawling and rolling about.
The holy man was greatly astonished at this. Convinced that it was God’s will, he agreed to baptize him.
There was no one with him except Abba Pior, whom he had just welcomed, and he was not a cleric but a layman.
Nevertheless, because of the necessity, he asked him to hold the baby above the basin so that he could pour the water over him. When he came forward to hold him,
he saw the grace of the priesthood above the blessed man’s head. He became frightened and fled, crying out, “Oubsais! Oubsais!”
This means, “My lord! My lord!” The blessed man caught hold of him and, with difficulty, persuaded him to assist him in the holy rite,
saying to him, “Do not fear condemnation on the grounds that you are unworthy. This is being done out of necessity, according to God’s will,
so that this faithful and hospitable man who welcomed us may be worthy of your blessing and of the grace that comes from God.”
50[?]. This same Abba Pior once had a vision in which he saw a large crowd of monks carrying one great cross on their shoulders at its two ends, turned backward toward one another.
Some were pulling this way, and the others in the opposite direction. They were obstructing one another and being obstructed by one another.
This signified the division that has now arisen through the dispute and conflict between the orthodox monks of Egypt and Palestine.
Both sides thought, because of their great zeal and their insistence on precision, that they were fighting for the truth.
An elderly man among the saints, Abba Lucius of the Cells, also foresaw this in the Spirit and made it known, saying to those with him:
“If some of you remain alive, you will reach a time when two men will be arrested to suffer martyrdom for Christ and for orthodoxy, yet they will not be in communion with one another.”
51. Likewise, the blessed Urbicia, whom we mentioned above, saw a fearful vision that signified this very thing.
For she saw herself going up at night, as was her custom, to the Church of the Holy Ascension, to worship alone in silence.
As she bent down on the steps, she saw in the portico before the Church of the Holy Ascension a woman dressed in purple garments.
She was shining there in the narthex. Trembling with fear, Urbicia fell on her face and lay on the ground.
But the holy Mother of God—for it was she—came forward and helped her stand up, saying, “Do not be afraid, mother. Do not be alarmed.”
Taking her by the hand, she walked about with her. Shining with light, she looked down from the portico, gazing at the mountain.
She said to Mother Urbicia, “Do you see, servant of God, what the mountain is like? Has it ever looked like this to you?
Tell me how you see it.” She replied, “I see the whole mountain as though it were made of split pieces of wood.”
The Mother of God said, “Look, just as you see this mountain, so from now on the Church of God will be divided until the end.”
52. Leontius was one of those considered to belong to a distinguished and prominent family of Ascalon. Eventually he renounced the world and became a monk and an abbot.
The holy Zeno, the desert dweller, prophesied to him, “You will become a bishop, but you will not die a bishop.”
When he became bishop of Ascalon, in accordance with the prophecy, he sought to gain the friendship and patronage of Nestorius the heretic,
who then controlled the church of Constantinople. He was entirely defiled by partiality and worldly thinking.
Consequently, when the wicked Nestorius was exiled, he sent him tributes and gifts in exile.
Afterward, when the Council of Chalcedon took place, he too went up. As people used to say, he was the one who, more than anyone else, urged [?] Juvenal to put his hand to the denial of the faith.
When the people of Ascalon learned this, they were filled with zeal and prepared not to receive him when he returned,
but either to drive him out or to stone him. For this reason, when he returned and reached Ascalon at night,
knowing the zeal of its people, he turned back to Cyprus. When he died there, his followers took his body and secretly tried to bring it to Ascalon
and bury it there at night. They found a ship sailing from the imperial court and put him aboard it.
On the ship there was also the body of a charioteer who was himself from Ascalon and had been summoned to Constantinople.
There he had displayed his professional skills with distinction. When he died, his people coated him with honey
and placed him in a lead coffin. They were bringing him back to his own people. But a violent storm arose at sea, and the waves surged up,
placing those aboard in danger of death. The sailors brought out cargo and threw it overboard, seeking to lighten the ship.
Along with everything else, they decided to throw out the charioteer’s body too and retain only the bishop’s,
out of respect for the episcopal office. But God’s justice was directing events: as the sailors were thrown into confusion by the waves and the storm,
they threw Leontius’s body into the sea instead of the charioteer’s. When they had sailed on and reached Ascalon, they quietly summoned the members of Leontius’s household.
They took the body at night, before anyone in the city could learn of it, and hurried to perform his funeral.
When they opened the coffin to bury the body, they found the charioteer in his full outfit, with a helmet on his head, holding his whip and girded with straps.
Ashamed, they ordered those present not to let anyone know at all. Instead, they conducted the charioteer’s funeral procession as though it were the body of Bishop Leontius.
They said that he was a good man, that he greatly loved giving alms, and that he kept the commandments.
And so the prophecy of Saint Zeno was fulfilled. I also heard many others confirm these things.
The God-fearing Abba Zechariah, the priest, used to speak about Zosimus, who was the head of the community at Ascalon.
He himself told me, affirming that through that very vision he had received full assurance. For he was a relative of Leontius.
Along with these others who were secretly summoned to his burial, he was an eyewitness and a witness to these things.
53. The abba said: “Three years before the Council of Chalcedon took place,
I was together with the blessed Theodotus and some of the fathers in Jerusalem. At about the seventh hour of the day,
we all clearly saw three suns in the sky: one in the east, another in the west, and another in the middle of the sky.
What that power and that vision were, God alone knows. But the outcome of events certainly makes it known.”
54. The abba said: “While I was in Egypt, at the time when there died in Constantinople as a martyr for the truth
the blessed Theodosius, archbishop of Jerusalem, I saw him that very night ascending to heaven, clothed in a white robe,
the kind that the bishops of Jerusalem customarily wear when they baptize. It was radiant and flashing with light, until he entered heaven.
I noted the day, and later, when his death became known, I found that it was the very day on which I had seen that vision.”
55. To those who say to us, “The whole inhabited world receives communion in the churches,
and you alone, few as you are, are schismatics, yet you call yourselves orthodox and zealous for the truth,”
the fathers handed down to us this answer: “Remember how many tens of thousands there were, all of them estranged from God and transgressors.
They perished in the wilderness. Not only did they lose the eternal blessings, but through their wrongdoing they were also prevented from entering the promised land.
And Moses, both the lawgiver and the great prophet, admonished them, saying, ‘Do not follow the majority in doing evil.’
Again, in Persia, when all the captives from Judah bowed down to the king’s image, those three young men remained steadfast, neither turning aside nor transgressing.
Because of this, not only were they themselves glorified by God as they glorified him, but for the king himself and for many who were present at the time,
they also provided knowledge of God free from error. With whom, then, do you wish to be in fellowship
and to have your share—with Joshua son of Nun, Caleb son of Jephunneh, and those three young men in Babylon,
or with the whole world that bowed down to the golden image? Consider this same thing also concerning the great crowd that was at Chalcedon, at the council of those who denied the faith.
Concerning it, it is especially fitting to quote that priestly saying of Jeremiah the prophet: ‘Many shepherds have ruined my vineyard
and defiled my inheritance. They have turned my delightful portion into an untrodden wasteland.’ And again: ‘One person who does the Lord’s will is better than a thousand.’”
56. When the apostate Juvenal returned from the council of the oppressors, the holy orthodox fathers and the monks in Palestine decided to meet him on the road.
They would do everything they could to persuade him to recognize his error, set himself right, and remove the stumbling block from the world.
They also persuaded the blessed Abba Peter, who was then living in seclusion in the lavra of Maiuma, to go with them.
He hesitated, since he was not accustomed to leaving it, and because of the contact with worldly people, especially those belonging to the imperial retinue.
For Juvenal had many of these men coming down with him to assist and protect him. Our Savior appeared to Peter and said:
“I am being wronged, and my faith is being transgressed, while you seek your own honor and quiet!” Thus stirred, he got up and set out.
They all went joyfully, as though going to suffer martyrdom. When the fathers were speaking with the impious Juvenal,
the blessed monk Theodosius, who was later made archbishop in Jerusalem by the faithful,
was publicly rebuking him for the apostasy that had taken place at Chalcedon, as someone who had been present throughout and knew everything that had happened.
He was exposing Juvenal’s favoritism and apostasy. Juvenal became angry and ordered a certain man of the [?],
one of those accompanying him, to treat Theodosius insolently, as a troublemaker who opposed the emperor’s will. As the man was about to do this,
the blessed Peter blazed with zeal. He was still a monk and did not yet hold the high office of bishop, but through the power of prophecy he knew the man:
“Do you dare intervene in matters of faith, or even speak at all? Did you not do such and such last night? I am the least of all the holy men here.

Do you want me to speak, so that fire immediately comes down from heaven and destroys you and those accompanying you?” Then the man, filled with fear and trembling and recognizing who Peter was, fell at his feet,
begging him before everyone, “Forgive me, my lord Nabarnugius! I did not know that Your Holiness was here.” In this way Peter protected the blessed Theodosius.
The man no longer dared to say or do anything against the holy men. He took Juvenal and returned to Caesarea.
57. Abba Paul, the former sophist [?], who had been the companion in solitude of the elder Abba Andrew, the desert dweller, used to tell us:
“At the time of the Council of Chalcedon, there were two of us living in solitude: myself and my brother, whose name was Theosebius.
He was an eloquent man with extensive knowledge of worldly wisdom, and he was uncertain about the doctrine of these two natures.
He begged the Lord to grant him assurance through his grace about what he should think concerning this matter and whom he should follow:
those who refused to speak of two natures, or those who accepted them. Saint John the Evangelist appeared to him and said to him, ‘Theosebius,
he who was from the beginning, whom we heard, who was revealed to us, whom we saw with our eyes
and touched with our hands—the Word of life.’ Having thus received assurance and become firmly convinced, he became a herald of the truth.”
58. A certain Aeneas was a priest and steward of the holy church in Jerusalem. He withdrew after the apostasy and became a zealous defender of the orthodox faith.
He used to tell the blessed Abba Peter and Abba Stephen the priest that, when the council was held at Ephesus—the one at which the wicked Nestorius was rejected—
He went up there with Juvenal, and from then on, when he saw his great partiality and that he was ready to give in—
were it not that he was plainly held in check by the blessed Cyril and his burning zeal and boldness, and was afraid—
he no longer wished to receive Communion from his hands, since he was partial and a transgressor.
59. If those who acted treacherously at Chalcedon say to us, “On what grounds do you call us transgressors, or traitors?”
we say to them: “It is an apostolic rule that says, ‘For if I rebuild the very things I tore down, I show myself to be a transgressor.’
“You, then, who at Ephesus rejected Nestorius, that champion of two natures,
and in that very act demolished the claim that two natures should be spoken of, and anathematized those who dared or dare to think or teach this way—
how are you not guilty transgressors, when you rebuilt at Chalcedon the very things you tore down then,
because of human fear, ease, and the turmoil stirred up by the wicked emperor? And you received the wicked Theodoret and Ibas without a trial,
although they had been cut off and cast out because of this wickedness—not just once, but twice, three times, four times, and five.
“You fell into this very kind of transgression, tearing down wickedness and then rebuilding it. For, as I said,
after you tore down this wicked doctrine at the council in Ephesus, you rebuilt that very same doctrine at Constantinople,
together with Flavian, who taught two natures. Then again, a little later, at the second council held in Ephesus,
with the holy Dioscorus, the orthodox patriarch, presiding, and Juvenal together with an assembly of orthodox bishops,
you tore down that wickedness. And a short time later, you openly rebuilt that very same thing at the Council of Chalcedon.
And, as I said before, you received Theodoret and Ibas without a trial, although they had been cast out because of this wickedness.
“Then again, in the Encyclical issued in the days of the blessed Archbishop Timothy, you held that very same wickedness up to ridicule through a universal, worldwide repudiation.
And a little later you rebuilt it in what is called the Anti-Encyclical, fulfilling what was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah: ‘They taught their feet to wander,
and had no regard for Him who is.’ You became a reed shaken by the wind, blown about and tossed by every wind.
And you continually limp on both hips, and have never stood firm on the path of truth.
For it is about you that it is written, ‘I have hated those who commit transgression.’ And God declares concerning them, saying near the end of the prophet Isaiah:
‘You will go out and see the corpses of those men who rebelled against me. For their worm does not die, and their fire is not quenched,
and they will be a spectacle to all flesh.’ And it is not only because of these things that you are transgressors and are called such,
but also because you overstepped the boundary set by the first council at Ephesus, which deposed Nestorius.
It decreed that from then on no one, whether a bishop or a cleric, was permitted to set down, present, write, or compose another statement or teaching concerning the faith.
Apart from what was first established by the three hundred and eighteen bishops together with the Holy Spirit.
But those who dare to do anything of this kind shall be excluded: bishops from the episcopate,
and clerics from the clergy. Now those who assembled at Chalcedon knew this definition very precisely.
At first they immediately rose, unwilling to introduce anything of this kind, shouting aloud and crying out:
“Let no one produce another formulation! We neither attempt nor dare to do so. The fathers forbade it. What they established is sufficient.
We cannot say, think, or establish anything beyond these things. There is no authority for another formulation.
There is a canon that says that what has been established is sufficient.” Many statements like these are written in the records made at that time,
to rebuke and ridicule their partiality and their transgression. But as for their being anathematized by us,
another apostolic canon commands and says: “Whoever preaches to you a gospel other than what I preached to you, let him be anathema.”
And again: “Even if I, Paul, or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel other than what you received, let him be anathema.”
Therefore, because they preached to us something other than the gospel, and something different from what we received from the council of the three hundred and eighteen holy fathers,
and especially from the council at Ephesus, which deposed Nestorius and rejected the doctrine of two natures,
those who assembled at Chalcedon wickedly preached another, new formulation. By this they became liable to the apostolic anathema,
and they are rightly anathematized by all who fear God. Thus it is not on our own authority or by our own judgment that we anathematize them,
but in following the apostolic canons and the definitions of the holy fathers; and we regard them as transgressors and as subject to anathema.
60. A certain God-fearing man once saw in a vision an assembly of all the bishops, with Saint Paul the apostle standing in their midst.
He was crying out and saying: “Are these my instructions to you? Are these the covenants I established for you? Are these my commandments?”
After rebuking them, he said to them: “Take water and wash your faces from this jar.” For a jar full of water had been placed in their midst.
As they washed, all their faces were found to be leprous. He said to them: “So not one of you has been found clean!”
61. I hear that one of the saints spoke boldly before the wicked Marcian. While rebuking the doctrine of two natures,
he said to him plainly and devoutly: “I was close to Christ, and I went about with him everywhere.
When he performed miracles, healed, and taught; when he was insulted and persecuted; when he was arrested, scourged, crucified, and suffered;
when he was buried, rose, ascended, and sat at his Father’s right hand—I was with him everywhere. And the one whom I saw teaching, healing, and raising the dead,
that very same one I also saw growing tired, weeping, hungering, thirsting, and enduring these other sufferings.
I never saw two in him, one and another, but always the very same one doing both these things and those, suffering and being glorified.”
And one incarnate nature of God the Word. When that wicked man marveled at the man and was put to shame, he sent him away with honor and in peace.
62. There was also another servant of Christ named John Comtinus, one of the faithful in Alexandria.
He was disputing with his [?], who was one of the Syrian Nestorians and was wickedly steeped in the defilement of the two natures.
He said to him, “Do you confess that the holy Virgin is the Mother of God?” Then, when the other said, “I confess that she is the Mother of God and the Mother of Christ,”
he answered him, “What, then? Did she give birth to two or to one?” When the other was pressed, his mouth was stopped, so that those standing nearby and listening marveled
and praised God for the wisdom given to his servant in defense of the truth.
63. Abba John, the bishop known as “of the Diakonia” and abbot of the monastery in Egypt, was a holy and wise man.
He used to say about the Council of Chalcedon that this Jewish utterance was continually being addressed to Christ:
“Why do you, though you are a human being, make yourself God, making yourself equal to God?”
64. In Pamphylia, a layman named Marcian, a zealous adherent of the orthodox faith, rebuked the bishop of the city before the congregation because he was expounding the faith wrongly.
He was arrested by the governor and received terrible, severe blows on his back and belly, to the point of death.
He was then carried home, thought to be dead. After a day, he was found to have nothing wrong with him. He told the faithful,
“After three lashes, I saw someone dressed in white clothes standing at my right hand, and from then on I no longer felt those blows.

Rather, it was as though they were touching me with [?].” A man who had suffered for many years from severe, incurable itching took some of the blood that had flowed from Marcian’s body and rubbed it on himself in faith. He was immediately cleansed of the disease.
65. When our blessed father, Abba Peter, became bishop, he took his seat in his church at Maiuma.
At that time Abba Isaiah the solitary, while secluded in his cell, saw the following vision:
There was a great, high, stinking dungheap in the middle of the inhabited world, occupying almost all of it and driving many people away with its stench.
An angel came down from heaven holding a shovel and said to Abba Peter the bishop, “Take this spade from me
and cleanse the inhabited world of the stench, for you have been commanded to free it.” The holy man hesitated and said,
“I cannot do this. The task is beyond my strength and, to put it more generally, beyond human strength.”
The angel did not stop pressing him until he compelled him to take the shovel to cleanse the inhabited world. When Abba Isaiah had seen these things,
he left his cell early in the morning and came to the blessed man at Maiuma. When he saw him, they exchanged blessings, and he recounted this vision to him.
Then he returned to his cell. What the outcome of this vision would be is known only to God, who alone is wise and knows everything.
The time to come will certainly also make it known. 65. The blessed Timothy, archbishop of Alexandria and confessor,
while he was in Cherson, related this to Abba John, who had been sent to visit and comfort him by the orthodox fathers in Palestine and by Abba Peter the bishop. He said:
When the Council of Chalcedon assembled, I saw in a vision that a service was being held in the church of Alexandria. When I approached to receive communion,
the bread turned out to be soot, and the wine vinegar. These signified the abandonment by God's grace that was about to come upon the churches.
66. This too Archbishop Timothy related to the man: “When the blessed Dioscorus was about to go to the council, I saw a vision like this:
the blessed Dioscorus entered the martyr's shrine of Saint John the Baptist to bid him farewell before departing and to receive a blessing from him.
After the prayer, he went up the steps to sit down, as was customary. When he sat down, all the clergy turned away from him and abandoned him.
But I alone followed him. As I was following him, a large, savage wolf suddenly encountered us and rushed at Saint Dioscorus.
It seized him by the neck and kept biting him. But since it had no teeth, it did him no harm. Then I saw a soldier appear and kill that savage wolf.”
It is clear that this wolf was Proterius.
67. Archbishop Timothy also related this to the man:
“It seemed to me,” he said, “that at that time I saw a wild and vicious horse. It was kicking with its feet and throwing the inhabited world into turmoil.
While everyone was fleeing from it, I alone took courage and confronted it. When I had overcome it by God's power, I bound it and shut it up in a cell.
It was never seen again.” This was, then, the wicked Marcian and his death through God's wrath.
68. He also related another vision to him, one that Proterius himself interpreted for him while he was still a cleric with him.
“I saw,” he said, “a tyrant enter the church and fight with everyone. He struck some and pursued others.
Some he killed, and others he insulted. I became indignant and could not endure such lawlessness and fighting.
I was strengthened by the Lord, took courage, approached him, and angrily drove him out of the church.
The next day,” he said, “as I was relating the vision to the clergy, Proterius, who was nearby, answered and said, ‘After Saint Dioscorus,
a heretic will take possession of the churches. You will drive him out and become bishop in his place.’”
69. Proterius himself used to say to one of the holy women
that at the time when news of the deposition and exile of the blessed Dioscorus reached Alexandria, “I said that whoever succeeds Dioscorus
is the Antichrist.” She therefore reproached Proterius to his face with these very words. After suffering much at his hands, she won the crown of the confessors.
70. My brother, the blessed Evagrius, while he was still in communion with the bishops, left Beirut with Zechariah, Antelaus, and Philip to renounce the world.
He came to Tyre, to Abba Elijah the priest, and there received assurance concerning the orthodox faith.

When he was about to anathematize the Council of Chalcedon the next day and receive communion from him, he saw that night, he said, that there was something foul on his tongue, like an old, rotten fishhook.
Immediately he spat it out and was healed. The next day, as I said, when he was about to receive communion and anathematize the council, he remembered his dream.
For this foul itch signified the corruption of these two natures.
71. The power of a dream was also experienced by brother Anastasius, a monk from Edessa, who had been a lawyer. For while he was still in Beirut,
and was receiving communion from the unbelievers, he saw an old and holy man, a [?], who said to him, “If you want to be saved, get yourself a horse
and hurry to Bishop Peter the Iberian. From him you will receive the true seal and be saved.”
“Immediately,” he said, “I shook off everything and came to the father, who was then at Aphthoria with Father Gregory.”
He told him about this vision and about many more visions he had seen while he was in Antioch and during his journey up, which had indicated beforehand
that he should withdraw from the world and had called him to depart and flee completely from this world. He was persuaded, made his request, and was received by him.
He was instructed in the true faith, and after anathematizing the Council of Chalcedon, he became a monk with him and withdrew from the world.
He used to tell us that, on the night before he was to receive communion, “I seemed,” he said, “to see myself
like someone newly baptized, wearing a splendid robe, with many people walking ahead of me carrying candles.
While I was inwardly puzzled and wondering how this had happened to me, since I had already been baptized once in childhood,
I saw the old man whom I had seen in Beirut. He said to me, ‘Do not be afraid or puzzled. This is not a second baptism.
Rather, all those who become orthodox are found worthy of light like this, and of glory and splendor.’”
72. The very same vision was also seen by the Christ-loving Gaianus, who was one of the leading members of the governor’s staff.
He was from Sebaste in Palestine, where the body of Saint John the Baptist lies.
For when he met the blessed Bishop Peter, he was instructed by him and received a precise understanding of the orthodox faith.
When he was about to anathematize the Council of Chalcedon and enter into communion with the saints, he saw himself in a vision at night dressed in white,

with many people walking ahead of him carrying torches and lights, as before someone being baptized. Thus persuaded, he withdrew from communion with those who had been excluded, and became orthodox and zealous.
73. Zacharias the lawyer, who was from Maiuma, was orthodox, very zealous, and precise in matters of doctrine, so that he was now also able to help others.
While he was in Beirut, he saw himself, he said, as though he were in the church of those who were in communion there.
“As the service was being completed,” he said, “and the deacons were distributing the cup, they were not saying any holy and sacramental words,
but instead something else, ugly and indecent.” While he was disturbed and alarmed,
he saw Abba Isaiah, the father of the monks, whom he knew—for he had seen him very often—saying to him, “Flee from the church of these Quaternitarians and separate yourself from them.”
74. A God-loving priest of the Alexandrians named Themison, a man renowned for chastity and modest conduct, told us that when Salophaciolus took control of the church in Alexandria,
“I was then,” he said, “a deacon of the church of Naracrora. I had charge of the sacristy and was entrusted with the [?] used in the service. Out of necessity, I used to stay there and sleep there.”
The bishop of that city had been driven out by its inhabitants as a heretic. When Salapiuris left, he took him along so that he could return and take possession of the church.
As for me, as I said, since I was in charge of the sacristy, I decided to wait for his arrival and first hand over every one of the vessels to him, and in this way escape slander and oppression.
That very night, while I was sleeping in the sacristy, I saw great crowds of saints dressed in white, and the holy Mother of God was standing among them.
She was hurrying to leave that place. It was as though a she-donkey had been brought, beautifully and modestly saddled, and she sat on it after the saints helped her mount.
When she was about to leave, with the saints going ahead of her, she looked at me as she sat on the donkey and beckoned to me with her hand.
She called me and said to me, “Leave this place, do not delay, and follow me.” For this reason, this man, who had been ordained a priest, came to Alexandria.
He was greatly loved by the orthodox fathers. When the holy bishop Timothy returned,
he found great favor with him, since he was an outstanding orthodox man, adorned with other virtues as well. Timothy kept him there, and he distinguished himself in the faith to the end,
both while the blessed Timothy was still alive and after his death, gathering the people together, strengthening them, and building them up until his last breath.
75. He also said this: “When, as I said, that heretical bishop was about to come to Rhinocorura,
all of us who were orthodox clergy decided to leave before his arrival.
Now one of the city's inhabitants had an infant who had not been baptized, and he was pleading for the child to be baptized by the orthodox,
before that heretic arrived and he was subjected to coercion in the matter. When the baptism was completed,
the infant being baptized cried out during his baptism, ‘Catch it! Catch that dove flying away and escaping!’ It was, in fact, the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove.
He appeared then and showed that, after the heretics take possession, the grace of the Holy Spirit departs and abandons the churches.”
76. Abba told us: “When we were living in the port of the city of Jamnia, at the time when Proterius was in Alexandria,
I had a friend who was a cleric. At first he was thought to be orthodox and zealous.
Eventually he became close to Proterius and became general administrator and superintendent of church affairs, conducting himself with great ostentation.
Once, when I was hurrying to visit one of the saints, he encountered me in a narrow place in the city, accompanied by a grand procession.
When I saw him, I wanted to turn aside, but I could find no suitable place, so I turned my face toward the wall.
But when he saw and recognized me, he ran toward me and greeted me. I, flustered and at the same time feeling compelled,
turned and returned his greeting, saying, ‘Give me your blessing.’ He said to me, ‘Why are you running away from me? Am I not your friend? What wrong have I done, that you have turned away from me?’
I said only this to him: ‘You know what you have done,’ and went past him. That very night I saw a great plain filled with light and heavenly glory,
with crowds of saints and ranks of angels praising and glorifying God, and the Lord himself in their midst.
When I saw him, I ran toward him to bow down before him, eagerly pressing forward, with presumption in my mind.
For I was very familiar with him and could speak freely with him. But when he saw me from a distance coming toward him in sorrow, he turned his face away from me before all the saints, distressed.
So all the saints were astonished. But I immediately understood that the reason for this was
the encounter—that is, the conversation—that I had had with that unbeliever. I fell down in tears, saying:
“My lord, have mercy on me. You yourself know, you who know hearts, that it was not wholeheartedly or willingly
that I did this, but because I was pressed and hurried into it.” Only with difficulty, when all the saints pleaded on my behalf, was he persuaded to receive me.
77. The abba also told us this about Serapion the lawyer, a very faithful man, zealous for orthodoxy, a lover of the saints, and the foremost of the lawyers in Alexandria.
In the time of Proterius, he gave shelter to the saints who were being persecuted everywhere and provided for their expenses from his earnings.
For this reason he was found worthy of the following divine vision. For when the authorities of Alexandria,
to please Proterius, drove all the orthodox clergy and monks out of the city

and out of the surrounding monasteries, none of the saints dared to appear and celebrate the Eucharist for the faithful, even when Easter, the feast of the Lord celebrated throughout the world, arrived.
The lawyer Serapion mentioned above was hiding in his house for fear of the unbeliever. He was in great distress and anguish of soul because he was deprived of Communion
on such a holy day. When the hour arrived on the holy night at which they customarily held the holy assembly,
he went outside into his courtyard under the open sky. He knelt down in tears, praying and pleading with God, with his hands stretched out toward heaven.
While he was praying, as he was about to finish his prayer and lower his hands, a portion of the Lord’s body was found in his hand. When he partook of it,
he was so strengthened and confirmed in the faith that he was found worthy to go up to Constantinople in chains, having been handed over by Proterius to Marcian,
and to receive the crown of the confessors. Indeed, when he went up to Constantinople, he was granted still greater grace and help from our Lord.
For he appeared before the emperor as so clearly [?] that he was permitted to live in Constantinople openly and without fear, and to be enrolled among the lawyers there
and hold the foremost rank. There he ended his life.
78. Some orthodox lawyers from Alexandria were studying in Beirut.
They went with others to a certain stylite who lived in a village near the city. He heard that they did not receive Communion from the church or the bishops,
from others who told him this about them. He became angry and said to them, “Where do you receive Communion
while you are away from home?” They replied openly, “We have the Eucharist from our holy orthodox fathers, and we partake of it.”
He said to them, “How is it proper for you, as laypeople, to give yourselves permission to take Communion?”
They said to him, “Our fathers, who are strictly orthodox clergymen, have expressly permitted us to do this,
since it is permissible and fitting.” When they returned to Beirut and Sunday came, one of them was in doubt.
As he recalled the words of that stylite, who had received some of that holy offering from him personally. Finally, after rebuking himself and gaining strength through faith, he approached.
When he received the burning coal, a clot of blood was found in his hand. That lawyer himself related this miracle to us, for he eventually became a monk as well.
79. The blessed priest Stephen, who had been an archdeacon in Jerusalem, was a zealous orthodox believer.
He had a holy sister who, during these holy forty days of fasting, went out once a week.
Throughout the rest of the year, [?]. She frequently visited the shrines of Saint Stephen and Saint John the Baptist.
There she kept vigil. She attained such a degree of holiness and purity that she saw Saint Stephen and Saint John in person.

They came to her, spoke with her, and blessed her. When the Council of Chalcedon took place, she began to hesitate about continuing her customary visits to the martyrs’ shrine and praying with the wrongdoers,
and especially with Juvenal the apostate, who then controlled the church. While she was distressed that she would be separated from the company of the saints,
Saint Stephen appeared to her and said, “Go and remain quietly in your cell. Do not compromise your conscience, and do not be distressed
as though you were being separated from us. Wherever you are, we will come there and make our dwelling with you.”
80. A certain orthodox woman from Pamphylia renounced the world together with her daughters, came to Jerusalem, and took up a life of solitude on the Mount of Olives.
Once, when she went up to worship at the holy place of the Ascension, it happened that a service was being held there that very day. Without her knowing it, the doors were shut.
Unable to leave, she stood hidden beside a pillar until the service ended.
Then she returned to her cell, to her daughters. Later, when she fell ill with the illness from which she died,
and was close to death, she cried out, saying, “Come and see what an accusation they are bringing against me at this hour!
They say, ‘How can you now be justified or be among the orthodox—you who, while a service was being conducted by these apostates,
chose to remain and watch these unworthy men giving the mysteries to people even more unworthy than themselves?’”
Her own orthodox son, who was a deacon named Theodulus, told us this.
81. He also added this: once this same woman saw herself being brought before the throne of God as though for judgment.
She heard a voice coming to her from within the throne: “Do you confess that the Son of God was born of the holy Virgin Mary, the Mother of God?
Do you confess that the Son of God was crucified and suffered for us?” And so, after she confessed, she was accepted and deemed worthy of his love for humanity.
82. In Attalia in Pamphylia there was a certain abbess named Zota, who directed a convent of orthodox virgins.
She was very pure in her conduct and her thoughts, and practiced great ascetic discipline.
Once, while she was in a trance after the reversal of the Encyclical, she saw herself in Paradise, with the tree of life in its midst.
Many bees were flying about and striving to taste from the tree, but they were not allowed to do so. It was as though an attendant were driving them away.
who was dressed in white and stood beside the cross, driving them away with his stole. When she asked him why he was driving them away,
he said to her, “Because these are the ones who, after the reversal of the Encyclical, assented to the Council of Chalcedon.”
On another occasion, when Claudianus, the bishop of Italy, came to this woman and was reproached by her for having signed the so-called Anti-Encyclical, he became agitated and said,
“I wrote with my hand, not with my soul or my heart.” She said to him, “And how can the hand move
unless the soul first wills it and moves it? Can a dead person move? Neither, then, can a hand move without the soul.”
83. Abba Leontius, the superior who came from Lycia and was renowned everywhere.
When the so-called Anti-Encyclical and the reversal of the orthodox Encyclical were about to take place, he saw in a vision that the altar of the church was being stripped
and the consecrated gifts were thrown on the ground [?]. Because of this, he testified to everyone, saying, “I will no longer assent to the church of those who make God a quaternity.”
84. Another of the holy men saw, at that same time, the church as though it were a stable, with various kinds of irrational animals there and a great deal of filth.
85. The blessed Epictetus was the abbot of the great monastery of the orthodox and a zealous man in Pamphylia. As Bishop Epiphanius told us—
he had also been his disciple and successor—Epictetus once said that, while in a vision, he had seen Amphilochius, the bishop of Side, who was considered merciful
and whose conduct was blameless and whose faith was orthodox. Nevertheless, he had signed the Tome of Leo and participated in the proceedings of the Council of Chalcedon.
With him he saw Epiphanius, the bishop of Perge, both of them buried in mud up to their necks.
Abba Epictetus said to Amphilochius with tears, “How is it that you,
who shone so brightly in a life of virtue, have been found in this mud?” He answered him, “If there is anything good, it comes from God.
But if there is sin, it comes from us. I am suffering these things, my lord abba, because of the Council of Chalcedon, to which I assented.”
86. A certain modest and highly regarded woman in Alexandria, whose name was Agathocleia, was uncertain after the reversal of the Encyclical
about how she ought to receive communion. She earnestly asked the Lord about this, seeking what she called full assurance.
She was heard because of her great chastity, and she saw in a vision a large church with two altars in it. The larger one was plain and bare,
and one of the bishops who were in communion with the Council of Chalcedon, whom she knew, was standing at it, ministering and offering the sacrifice.
The other altar, on the right, was small in size, but it was adorned with much gold and precious stones and shone brightly.
A little child was standing at it and offering the sacrifice; he was the Lord himself. He said to her, “Receive communion from here.” Having thus been assured,
she praised God and kept away from the communion of those who profess two natures. Thus she remained firmly orthodox and discerning in her life and faith.
87. In the monastery of Abba Romanus there were two brothers who were natives of Pelusium and belonged to the city's leading families,
John and Timothy. While the blessed Romanus was still alive, they renounced the world and received from him, so to speak, the monastic habit.
A long time after the death of Abba Romanus, Timothy, one of them, grew weak during his final illness. When he died,
the brothers took him, as was customary, washed him, and laid him on a bench, preparing to bury him. But suddenly he sprang up and sat.
While everyone was marveling and stood in amazement, a large crowd of monks came running with the abbot of that time. They asked him whether he had really died
and how he had risen after dying. He told them that he had truly died and had been carried to the place of judgment and justice and brought before the Judge.
As he said these things, he wept bitterly, sighed, and cried out, saying, “Oh, the strictness! Oh, the strictness!
Oh, the strictness! You yourselves are my witnesses to how careful I was, while I was with you, not to offend the conscience of any brother.
Even though I was negligent in everything, nevertheless I could find mercy and help from nowhere at that hour, nor escape torment,
except because I had kept the true faith undefiled and, from my youth until this very hour, had kept myself away from communion with the deniers at Chalcedon.”
88. Something like this happened in Antioch the Great, which I myself witnessed. Having learned of it firsthand,
I thought it necessary to set it down alongside the accounts written above, for the faith and full assurance of many.
There is an imperial palace in that city which, according to those who have seen it, is not inferior
in beauty, size, and its other splendid grandeur to the palaces in Rome and Constantinople.
It has been closed for some time because it is not needed, and is merely kept under guard in case the emperor should happen to visit these parts.
A man wearing the plain clothing of an ordinary person came to its great gate, the outermost of all, which was closed, as I have said.
He made himself a little shelter against the gate itself and lived quietly in it summer and winter, in frost and nakedness.
For he had nothing but a single tunic. He maintained silence and spoke nothing with his mouth.
For many years he remained there, praying with sighs and tears. He never wished to accept anything from anyone:
gold or silver, or even copper coins. But a fuller, a neighbor of his who had a shop there,
would bring him a little bread, a stew of vegetables or pulses, and water toward evening. After taking what he needed, he would keep whatever remained
and give it to the poor who regularly came to him. He stood as a kind of example to the world.
When I heard these things about him, I became eager to visit him.
But I hesitated, lest it might displease the old man and I should go and trouble him. Nevertheless, after calling upon our Lord, I went to him.
When he saw me, he welcomed me warmly and looked at me with a cheerful face. I saw that he was a man in the middle years of old age, upright and thin.
His face was gaunt and wasted from mourning, tears, and ascetic discipline. When I found favor with him,
I sought to learn from him: “Why, since you love the ascetic life, do you live not rather in the wilderness or in a monastery, but in such a splendid and magnificent city?”
And you have made yourself a shelter in the marketplaces and in inclement weather.” But he, in silence, stretched his right hand toward heaven and indicated by a gesture
that “God commanded me.” When I asked him, “Why are you weeping?” and he gave no answer, I ventured to say to him:
“This is what I think: the time of the end has arrived, and you have been sent as a witness to us, to proclaim this to the world in this place.”
But he only shed tears. Many times I came to him to experience his modesty, and I was admonished merely by seeing him,
if indeed I had the sense to accept correction. He was also orthodox in faith and zealous.
He strongly denounced the Nestorians and turned his face away from them. Finally, as I heard after I had left, it was at their hands that
he was battered with severe blows. Weakened by those blows, he met his end in martyrdom.
89. At that same time there was a bishop of Qinnasrin named Nonnus, who had taken up the yoke of monastic life from his youth.
He practiced great austerity in the large and well-known monastery called that of Abba Acacius, beside the city. Eventually he became the guide and abbot of that monastery.
In the time of Martyrius, the Nestorian bishop who was driven from Antioch because of his open heresy, when many disputes were taking place in the city,
the previously mentioned Bishop Nonnus showed his zeal while he was still an abbot. He took the brothers of his monastery and came to Antioch.
He gave great assistance to the orthodox until the heretic Martyrius was driven from the city. Consequently, wishing to reward him for his zeal and diligence,
Peter, who was the bishop of the orthodox in Antioch at the time of the Encyclical, made him bishop of Qinnasrin.
Because he had an unusually great affection for me, he heard from me about the previously mentioned old man, who had taken up residence beside that palace.
When he learned that I knew him, he urged me to take him along with me to visit him, so that he could converse with him. As we were going toward his shelter,
I said to the bishop, “Wait here a little while, until I go ahead and find out what the old man is doing, lest he be standing in prayer and we disturb him.
At the same time I will tell him about your God-loving self.” When I went over and found him praying, I waited until he finished. When he had finished, I went in.
While I was still speaking to him, Bishop Nonnus, seeing that I was delayed, came up and began knocking from outside, wanting to enter.
I recognized him, and said to the old man, “This is the man about whom I spoke to your God-loving self.”
I got up and welcomed the bishop. As soon as he entered, the old man looked at his face, became filled with anger, and began blowing in his face repeatedly,
so that both I, in my embarrassment, and the bishop himself became greatly distressed and ashamed.
I pleaded with the old man and begged him not to do this, saying, “He is a bishop, a zealous man, and he has worked very hard for orthodoxy.”
But he kept blowing at him, stretching out his hand toward him and shaking it threateningly. He displayed great anger and kept saying,
“This man! This man!” Finally I took the bishop and went out in embarrassment, so as not to disturb the old man any further. I was greatly astonished,
wondering why the old man had become so agitated toward Nonnus, and what he had seen in him. Finally, from the outcome of events,
I made known [?] the reason. For this very man was so zealous and ascetic, and was regarded as a champion of the orthodox.
In the days of Calendion, the unholy, filthy heretic, he transgressed against the faith and became his associate. He became a source of grief and disgrace to the orthodox.
He was so impious as to call Christ a man clothed in God, and a man who was assumed, and to say that the holy Virgin gave birth to Christ.
And confusion, mixture, and a doubling of Christ himself, and other things like these, which our orthodox fathers subsequently rejected.
Although these expressions may have been used in simplicity by some of the holy fathers, it was not to indicate two sons, or persons, or Christs, or natures,
but to establish and confirm the true and complete incarnation, as we learn from their many writings and compositions.
Nevertheless, because of these heretics, who readily seize upon expressions like these,
as though they fully supported their false teaching, the orthodox fathers rejected them, as I said.
Likewise, they refused to speak of two natures after the union. They also refused to say, when distributing the holy gifts, “The body of Christ,” using that expression alone.
Instead, they said, “The body of God the Word,” and “The body of Christ, God the Word and our Savior,” as the blessed Cyril taught in his explanation of the eleventh chapter.
And likewise the blessed Timothy, in the discourse he composed against Leo’s Tome and the Council of Chalcedon.
For some of the clergy of Antioch reached such a degree of impiety while the heretic Martyrius still held control of the church,
that they dared to say, when distributing the holy gifts, “The body of the righteous man”—that bare expression. To these people it is right to apply the apostle’s saying,
which runs as follows: “For if anyone who transgressed the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses,
how much harsher a punishment do you think someone will receive who has trampled on the Son of God and regarded the blood—the blood of his covenant—as like anyone else’s,
by which we were sanctified, and has insulted the Spirit of grace?” Admirable is God’s declaration and testimony to the whole inhabited world,
which came from God to the holy Joshua son of Nun, who inherited the leadership and the gift of the great Moses.
For after those great miracles performed by God in Egypt,
and at the sea and in the wilderness, after that manna, after many great victories, after the crossing of the Jordan in a manner worthy of God,
after the capture of Jericho and the fall of its walls at the people’s shout alone, and its complete destruction under the ban—after all these miracles,
because of the sin of one man who transgressed God’s command and took something, stealing from what was under the ban, God became angry with the whole people.
Israel was defeated by a few enemy fighters, so that many of them fell, and the whole people were filled with fear and terror.
The people themselves lost hope, as did even the great commander Joshua. For it is written that the people’s heart trembled and became like water.
Let us therefore hear the accounts that follow these events in the Holy Scriptures, which continue as follows: “Joshua tore his clothes and fell facedown on the ground until evening,
he and the elders of the people. They put dust on their heads. Joshua said, ‘I beg you, my Lord, why bring this people across the Jordan, only to hand them over to the Amorites?’
so that they might destroy us. If only we had stayed and settled beside the Jordan! What can I say, now that Israel has turned its back on its enemy?
When the Canaanites and all those who live in the land hear about it, they will surround us and wipe us off the land.
And what will you do for your great name? The Lord said to Joshua, “Get up! Why have you fallen on your face?
The people have sinned and broken my covenant, which I had established with them. They have stolen some of the things devoted to destruction and put them among their own belongings.

The Israelites can no longer stand against their enemies, because they themselves have become devoted to destruction. I will no longer be with them unless you remove from among you what is devoted to destruction.”
If, then, when one person out of this entire people broke God's commandment and sinned, great wrath came upon all the Israelites together,
now, concerning the foul-named council of Chalcedon, where there was an assembly of many bishops,
and not only an assembly of bishops, but also a multitude of peoples who, through them, committed injustice and transgressed—
they did not merely break an ordinary commandment, nor was it over a worldly matter. Rather, they denied the true faith in God itself and the confession of him, and came under the ban.
For they also fell under the ban pronounced by the blessed apostle and under the canons of the holy fathers
and the earlier holy councils. How, then, could they not rightly have called down God's wrath upon the whole earth?
Even now he says to them, “I will no longer be with you unless you remove from among you what is under the ban.”
The very outcome of events has clearly shown this. For, look, from that time onward the Roman Empire ceased and came to an end,
from the time when she became the source of evil and the abomination called Leo's Tome came out of her.
And she who had been the mistress and queen of the whole inhabited world became a captive, and barbarians gained power over her.
Jeremiah lamented over her and said, “How the city sits alone, she who was full of peoples!”
And again: “The chief among the provinces has become subject to tribute.” The great city, the crown of glory, the joy of the whole earth—all her splendor has been cast away from her.
“Jerusalem has sinned grievously; therefore she has become an object of horror, because the Lord has brought her low for her many wicked deeds,” because there is something under the ban among them.
Things like these the prophet Jeremiah lamented over her in prophecy, as did Isaiah when he said, “How the faithful city, Zion, has become a prostitute!
She was full of justice, and righteousness rested within her, but now there are murderers and those who transgress against the truth.”
Elsewhere he addresses them, pronouncing woe upon them: “Woe, rebellious children! You made a plan, but not through me, and a covenant, but not by my Spirit.”
